speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to propose a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The derailment in November, 1979 in Mississauga could well have turned out to be a national catastrophe. Clearly unsafe methods with respect to the movement of dangerous commodities by rail through built-up areas must be better regulated. The Grange report makes 15 recommendations to improve rail safety. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That this House do direct the Minister of Transport to implement forthwith the Grange report, not diddle around for another year, as he has indicated he will, with more studies but take rail safety seriously and show some respect for the safety of Canadians living near rail rights of way.

REQUESTED RESCISSION OF CORN COMPETITIVE FORMULA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek the support of this House in redressing an injustice to western farmers which has existed since 1974 when the Hon. Otto Lang forced the corn competitive formula for pricing feed grains on the producers. This corn competitive formula has had the effect of depressing feed grain sale prices and is costing the western producer millions of dollars each year. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That the government accede to requests from the Canadian Wheat Board, the United Grain Growers and other grain associations, individual producers and western members of Parliament, and rescind the corn competitive formula for
feed grain pricing to allow the price to float free and to allow the western producers to derive just returns for their grain.

speechtext:

Now that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been informed about the size and lethal nature of U.S. military aid to the junta in El Salvador, and in view of the Prime Minister's stated intention to meet with the new President of the United States in the near future, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that because of inflation Canada Savings Bonds no longer present an attractive investment for Canadians since banks and other financial institutions have a much more attractive rate of return for short and long-term investments, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That the interest received from Canada Savings Bonds and other federal government bonds be considered as dividends so that people purchasing such bonds can claim a tax credit on their income tax, similar to that which now applies to dividends paid by Canadian corporations to Canadian investors.
A positive move in this direction would not only substantially increase the sale of federal bonds, but would reduce to almost nil the redemption or cashing in of such bonds.

The $260 million the federal government is providing the Farm Credit Corporation is inadequate to meet its demands, and under the present high interest rate conditions many farmers are finding it very difficult to continue their operations. That extra money should be provided to the Farm Credit Corporation, possibly as much as $200 million, and interest rates for farmers borrowing this money be frozen at the existing rate of 12.75 per cent. If these measures are not taken, the survival of thousands of Canadian farmers is threatened.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The government announced yesterday that it intends to buy a $350 million band-aid to stick on communities that have been TKO'd through lost jobs. Not content with pillaging jobs from other areas and carrying them off to their own ridings-as the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister of State for Trade (Mr. Lumley) did when they snatched 200 jobs from Parks Canada in Peterborough and as the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) did when she snatched hundreds of jobs in east central Ontario by stopping the Eldorado Nuclear plant expansion in Hope township and moved it to her own riding-according to news reports this morning Windsor and Cape Breton are now front runners in this new Liberal sweepstake, so that areas where byelections are pending can count themselves lucky.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes):
That cabinet consider that its duty is to disburse these funds fairly, on the sole basis of need and beyond the scope of partisan bias. In this way they have an opportunity to redress in some measure their previous policies of pork-barrelling patronage.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my initial question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who announced yesterday with two fellow ministers a certain program which he described as being:
Oral Questions
-measures to respond to serious industrial dislocation situations. These measures will be made available in communities designated on the basis that they have recently experienced large scale industry dislocation that has directly resulted in a significant increase in the level of community unemployment.
Madam Speaker, my question to the minister is simply this: Why does he persist in coming forward with such ad hoc measures, in effect bringing in measures after the fact as opposed to bringing in a proper industrial strategy for this country? Why does he not bring in an industrial strategy which, as he told his interviewers in a recent interview, he feels rightly should take second priority to such things as the constitutional debate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY

Madam Speaker, what we announced yesterday, in my view and in that of the government, certainly should be one element of an industrial policy framework. What we announced is consistent with the need in this country right now to encourage industrial restructuring and the adaptation of labour to present and emerging situations in a way which will help bring about strong, permanent economic growth in ways which meet international competition.
I am sorry the hon. member does not agree with this but I think working people in his riding and across the country would agree with what we did yesterday in carrying out a commitment made in the budget of October 28.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Let me tell the minister that what workers in Canada want are jobs, not last minute aid programs such as he is suggesting.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport arising out of the commission by Mr. Justice Grange on railway safety resulting from the Mississauga mishap. While the minister wants to study the subject for a year, although it is obvious the recommendations of Mr. Justice Grange need to be implemented, will the minister immediately order the implementation of at least the first three of the recommendations of Mr. Justice Grange? Because if they are not implemented another 30 to 50 derailments will occur each year as a result of the wrong kind of equipment?
January 20, 1981

Madam Speaker, the premise is wrong, unfortunately. I never said this was a study group, and I never said it would report after a period of one year. The question raised by a member of the press was, how long did I expect the consultative committee to stay at work, and I said it might be a full year. This is an advisory committee, which is meeting for the first time next week. I will meet with it within four weeks. It will express to me in time a position on each one of these recommendations Justice Grange has made. We are going to make decisions very, very rapidly.
Justice Grange himself suggested a number of tests and a certain amount of research. The confusion created in respect of the one year is related simply to the suggestion that the committee will go on with these tests and do this research, which may take one full year. However, I repeat that decisions will come much faster than that.

Madam Speaker, there is no problem about the continuation of tests. The first three recommendations of Mr. Justice Grange have called for the minister to instruct- and he and two of his predecessors have been questioned about this repeatedly for the last several years-the CTC or to request the CTC to act in the same way it did-very quickly- after the Mississauga accident last year with respect to the consist of a train. The CTC acted very quickly then. Will the minister ask the CTC to act under section 227 or section 100 of the Railway Act? The authority is already there to require the railroads to begin immediately implementing the first three recommendations of Mr. Justice Grange.

Madam Speaker, I think it would be unwise and certainly not very polite to the members of the advisory committee which I have created-three of them outsiders to the government-if I were to start announcing seriatim decisions on the recommendations. I will do it in a very orderly fashion. I will receive their views beginning four weeks from now and act quite rapidly, as the hon. member will see, as the proper information is obtained and the proper assessment is made by this advisory committee with respect to each one of the recommendations.

Madam Speaker, the minister is still copping out. He is still acting like a sponge. Mr. Justice Grange and every recognized authority in transportation, including management, unions and experts in the field, know that technology has been in place for 30 years with respect to roller bearings and for a number of years with respect to hot-box detectors. Recommendations of the railway brotherhoods in connection with marshalling and consist of trains have been put before the minister and his predecessors repeatedly. He does not need another committee.
I would like to ask the minister if he will now call upon his colleagues and particularly the President of the Treasury Board-since Mr. Justice Grange was so critical of the restraint program-to stop the decrease in the number of
Oral Questions
safety inspectors, increase the budget of the CTC and increase the amount of training and the number of railway safety personnel.

Madam Speaker, I think any person with his head squarely on his shoulders-that would include the hon. member who is asking this question-would act the way I am acting in this matter. He would not on the basis of his own prejudices, knowledge or whatever decide on the day after the receipt of a document like this which of the recommendations to accept and which not to accept. That would be foolish. What I am doing now is the normal thing to do, and even the hon. member would do that if, incredible as it may seem, he were in my position.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The minister knows that in 1971, after 36 days of comprehensive hearings into a number of rail disasters, a whole series of recommendations were made. The inquiry was followed up and further reports were made in 1973. The minister knows from reading Mr. Justice Grange's report, which he has had for at least six weeks, that the CTC has been a sleeping policeman. Will the minister make changes in the personnel of the CTC so people can be satisfied that that organization, which is supposed to protect the interests of people generally, in fact works to do what it is supposed to do?

Madam Speaker, as the hon. member says, Mr. Justice Grange has analysed all that and has not been, shall we say, very laudatory with respect to the position of the CTC in some of these matters. However, he went on to say that there are preoccupations, which he respects, in relation to the economic viability of some of the existing regulations, and he suggests that the time has come when the onus must be tipped from the economic preoccupation more to the safety preoccupation, that a social change has taken place in recent years. He suggests that the time has now come to incorporate that change in the rules and regulations concerning train transportation and safety. It is difficult in this context to hold a number of people responsible for a change which had not taken place in society as a whole. It may be that the time has come to do that, and that will be indicated by our reaction to the recommendations which Mr. Justice Grange makes.

Am I to gather from the minister's answer that the CTC has been more involved in economics than in safety and that it has been in bed with the railways rather than doing its job of looking after the interests of individuals, of VIA Rail and so on? If that is the minister's view, surely it is time that the minister had a little purge.

Order.

My supplementary question, Madam Speaker, is in connection with the report. There are a number of things that could be done right now without a long study period. Will the minister order that trains carrying dangerous chemicals be no more than 4,000 feet in length? Will the minister order that dangerous chemicals be carried only in cars having roller bearings in their journal boxes? Will the minister order that the railways immediately commence installing heat sensors every 20 miles as recommended? In other words, will the minister take his responsibilities for safety seriously?

Madam Speaker, I am inferring two things. The first one is that the preoccupation with economics is not one that should be pushed aside easily. If the CTC had done that in the past, I suggest that my Conservative friend would have been one of the first to chastise them for having done so. Secondly, I suggest that a body of people, such as the Canadian Transport Commission, cannot be held solely responsible for the behaviour of society as a whole throughout the years. Realizing now that the situation has changed, that people have changed their minds, it may well be asked to take a position which would be slightly different from the one it took in the past.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING PROPOSALS TO ACHIEVE TARGET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Science and Technology. Yesterday the minister announced his increased commitment to research and development so that it could achieve 1.5 per cent of the gross national product by 1985. Unfortunately, the minister will remember that that was an announcement which was also made in 1978 for 1983. The reason that policy died is that the government did not bring forward any specific proposals for tax incentives and grants. I should like to ask what specific proposals or tax incentives and grants-that is, tax incentives for industries and grants to universities-is the minister bringing forward so that he can achieve the new target he set?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING PROPOSALS TO ACHIEVE TARGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, not only did I announce yesterday the target for reaching the objective of 1.5 per cent of the gross national product devoted to these efforts, but I also laid out the structure for planning purposes of proposed expenditures on the part of the federal government in the various areas in which it has concerns, such as support for universities, support for research in the private sector and support for the mission-oriented activities of federal government departments. Not only did we establish the target date; we indicated the kinds of expenditures which, for planning purposes, we thought would be necessary for achieving it. We also suggested that the percentage level of the federal government's effort within that 1.5 per cent target date should be .5 per cent.
I am using this planning structure as a basis for continuing discussions with the private sector and with the universities. Clearly it is not in its full form with a detailed nuts and bolts approach. Further programs will be brought forward to the government to indicate how we will achieve or hope to promote the kind of growth in the private sector, which is quite considerable, which will be necessary if we are to reach that 1.5 per cent target. I am sure the hon. member has already looked at the material which has been provided. It does much more than simply establish the target date of 1.5 per cent for 1985. A great deal more information has been provided about the government's targets in order to achieve that.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER HOSTAGE TAKING INCIDENTS WILL BE DISCUSSED AT HEADS OF STATE MEETING IN JUNE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his suggestion which I feel is excellent. Madam Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of State for Science and Technology. On numerous occasions I have asked the minister when he will present a detailed, long-term strategy which could achieve the goal of 1.5 per cent of our gross national product directed toward research and development, and the minister's statement in Toronto yesterday did not tell us anything new. It has been known for years that the reason we have had R&D expenditures similar to those of Portugal is that our private sector, mainly the multinationals, has a dismal record of research and development in this country. It has been known for years that the private sector must increase its R&D to some 27 per cent a year for the next five years if we are to achieve the goal-
Question.
Madam Speaker, my question is this.
Hear, hear!
Is there anything in the minister's statement that would force the multinational corporations to increase their research and development in this country, or is his statement just another pious hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course I am disappointed that the hon. member is not more enthusiastic about the statement I made, but I think, as I indicated in my response to the hon. member for Rosedale, there is a considerable amount of information and commitment in that statement which marks a significant step forward in our planning for science and technology research and development in the government. I indicated very clearly in my statement and in my discussions yesterday that the relatively poor performance in general of foreign-owned firms and subsidiaries in the research and development area is a matter of
Oral Questions
great concern to us and that we do have under consideration ways and means of trying to improve that performance. We are particularly anxious that foreign subsidiaries develop more than they have at present world product mandates.
The hon. gentleman asks what those steps are going to be. It was not my purpose yesterday to outline those details. I ask him to be content and to be patient for a little longer.

Madam Speaker, indeed, we have been waiting for a long period of time. The particular goal was announced in 1968 and it was announced again in 1978, but the announcements have all been pious hopes.
The other question I should like to direct to the minister concerns funding of universities. In the background paper which was provided with his speech, he suggested that the government's share of that 1.5 per cent was to be reduced to one third. However, he was also projecting an increase in the share of that projected goal by the universities. There is a contradiction there because the universities depend on government financing-
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Would the hon. member put his question.
How can the government increase the universities share of research at the same time as decreasing the federal government's share?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there are two principal ways in which the federal government assists universities. One is through the transfer of funds to provincial governments through established program financing arrangements for the support of post-secondary education. The other major instrument at our disposal is the activities of the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council. The hon. member will know that already this year we have very considerably increased the funds going to that council by something like $42 million. It is in the five-year plan of the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council that we hope to assist universities to meet the research and development obligations which we hope they will meet.

They have been instructed to be as humanitarian as possible within the realm of reason.

subsubtopic: APPLICATIONS BEFORE HERD MAINTENANCE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, one of the conditions in which cattlemen might qualify for assistance is that their crops would have to be less than 80 per cent of the average. Anyone who knows anything about agriculture-and I am sure the review board would know-would know that the yield one receives is in no way related to the crop yield or the yield of the hay crop because one can have a short-standing crop and a good yield, or conversely, a rank crop which lodges and there is no grain in it at all. Have any instructions gone out to change the particular criteria, which in a sense are ridiculous because many of the areas rejected were areas that did not receive freeze-out payments and simply do not have any cash to continue?

subsubtopic: APPLICATIONS BEFORE HERD MAINTENANCE REVIEW BOARD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I will know better when my colleague, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, returns to the capital later today from attending a meeting this morning in Regina, but I understand a lot of these matters have been considered. subsubtopic: SLAUGHTER OF CARIBOU HERDS-QUOTAS ON KILLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment. During this period last year thousands of Canadian caribou were slaughtered as the two main herds moved southward from the Northwest Territories into northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Will the minister tell the House what steps if any the government is taking to prevent such wanton destruction this year and in future years, especially in light of reliable reports that in 1980 frozen lakes were littered with crippled and dying animals and carcasses with often only the tongues or hind quarters removed? In fact, this was wanton destruction.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: SLAUGHTER OF CARIBOU HERDS-QUOTAS ON KILLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there have been meetings on the subject between my officials and representatives of provincial governments. An agreement under the Canada Wildlife Act between Canada, the Northwest Territories, Manitoba and Saskatchewan for co-operative action in establishing a migratory caribou board has been drafted by the Canadian Wildlife Service in Edmonton. The draft will be reviewed before the end of this month and after that it will be put in final form.

subsubtopic: SLAUGHTER OF CARIBOU HERDS-QUOTAS ON KILLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. In light of what the minister just said, could he confirm that the failure of the government to control the slaughter of Canada's two main barren ground caribou herds in the past has caused one herd to decline from 135,000 to 38,000 in the last eight years and the other to decline from 105,000 to 70.000 in the last two years? In light of that destruction, will the minister tell the House whether the program he just mentioned will involve instituting and enforcing quotas on kills so as to ensure the survival of this precious part of our country's natural heritage?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: SLAUGHTER OF CARIBOU HERDS-QUOTAS ON KILLS

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. It is further to the federal herd maintenance program. The chief criterion creating problems for the committee in western Canada at this time, about which the producers are complaining, is the provision requiring a crop of 80 per cent or less before farmers are eligible for the program. It happens to be a turning point for a great many people, which is why the appeal committee has so many appeals before it. Is the minister prepared to recommend to cabinet that the 80 per cent provision be done away with and the need be assessed for forage in each individual case as an alternative method?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):

Madam Speaker, this is the second time drought programs have run into administrative problems in western Canada. There was a committee which was supposed to keep them from running into problems. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROPOSED SERVICE BETWEEN OTTAWA AND NEW YORK CITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. It concerns the projected direct air connection between the national capital and the city of New York. My first question is with respect to time. There have been reports that it would take perhaps a year and a half before all the arrangements, both locally and internationally, can be made for that service to come to pass. Would the minister comment on that time frame and, if possible, would he be prepared to undertake to use his good offices at least here, if not in the United States, to shorten the time it will take before the final decision is made on this matter?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED SERVICE BETWEEN OTTAWA AND NEW YORK CITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the subject is very popular with Members of Parliament as well as diplomats and businessmen. As my hon. friend knows, there are two ways of dealing with the matter. One method is by way of amending the Canada-United States bilateral air agreement under which Eastern Airlines now holds the franchise. The other method of dealing with the matter is if both the Canadian regulatory agency and the American regulatory agency were to agree on one of the candidates. It is with regard to the second method that it has
Oral Questions
been said it might take up to one year and a half to complete the arrangements.
I am trying to deal with this particular problem as wisely as possible. I am exploring both avenues. My interest in this case is almost as great as, if not greater than, the interest of the hon. member. I have taken, first of all, the bilateral approach to find out if Eastern Airlines expect to offer their service. Secondly, if Eastern do not wish to offer service, which appears to be the case, I would like to determine if any other American carrier would be willing to take over the route and, if so, under what conditions. An agreement with the United States would follow if this approach were successful.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROPOSED SERVICE BETWEEN OTTAWA AND NEW YORK CITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister knows that there are two Canadian carriers which are interested in this matter. I hope that the minister will emphasize that aspect in his discussions and expedite those discussions as quickly as possible. But there is one question which arises with respect to this matter, and it is with regard to either the intervention or the proposed intervention by Air Canada for the purposes of preserving a right rather than providing a service, as is the intent of the other two air carriers.
Would the minister be prepared to use his good offices to ask Air Canada if it has filed a request with the board to withdraw and, if it has not, to request that Air Canada not intervene so that an already tedious process, as the minister has described it, will not be made even more tedious? Would the minister give that undertaking to the House?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED SERVICE BETWEEN OTTAWA AND NEW YORK CITY

Madam Speaker, I will bear in mind what the hon. member has asked, but I would also like him to bear in mind the fact that I must work within the existing agreement between Canada and the United States. As much as I would like to be sympathetic toward the Canadian carrier, I must keep this fact in mind. 1 must also keep in mind the apparent preference of Ottawans for certain types of aircraft as opposed to other types.
On the subject of Air Canada, I must say that I have not gone into the details as to what has been said with regard to the requests of the two airlines, Air Atonabee and First Air, but I will do so and report to the hon. member at the earliest opportunity.

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION IN SAFETY PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the President of Transport arising out of the Grange report. The commission saw fit to devote one section toward the CTC's inaction in various areas related to safety, as have been referred to by my colleague and particularly with respect to the general safety inquiry between 1971 and 1973 wherein firm recommendations were made with

January 20, 1981
Oral Questions
respect to the installation of roller bearings, hot-box detectors and regulations with respect to speed. The commissioner pointed out that there was absolutely no action taken by the CTC in any of those areas. Such action would not require money and there would be no impact in so far as the restraint order is concerned.
It seems that the CTC is not fulfilling its rightful responsibility in the area of safety. Would the minister seize upon this opportunity, given the ammunition which is available in this report, to call in the CTC and remind it of its rightful responsibility and obligations in this regard so that we may improve the confidence in and reliability of safe rail transportation in this country?

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION IN SAFETY PROCEDURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I had been a lawyer and visiting the courts regularly, I would have tended to take the point of view that society as a whole tends to be guilty of sins of omission and commission more so than individuals or institutions. What I mean to say by that is that it is very difficult for me, and I would hope for my predecessor as well, to chastise an institution for its interpretation of events brought about as a result of social thinking which was not entirely or exclusively the thinking of the institution. That is the position which I take. Consequently, I am more interested in what we will do now than in what has been done in the past. I will act accordingly.

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION IN SAFETY PROCEDURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, certainly I am interested in what will happen in the future, but I wish that the minister would respond to my question. Will he call in the members of the CTC and remind them of their rightful responsibility under the provisions of the statute?

subsubtopic: ROLE OF CANADIAN TRANSPORT COMMISSION IN SAFETY PROCEDURES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I was intending to do that, but one of the members of the CTC is on the advisory committee which will be presenting its views to me. As I will exercise this responsibility personally, I will be in close contact with Mr. Gray regularly and will debate these points with him. One thing which impressed me in reading the report-and by the way I did not receive the report six weeks ago, but just on Sunday-is the balanced approach which Mr. Justice Grange takes in his report. For example, when he talks about speed he asks how we can talk about speed without taking into consideration the quality of the equipment, the training of people on the trains, and the safety devices, techniques and procedures which are used.

Madam Speaker, I have a couple of forestry-related questions which 1 would like to direct to the Minister of the Environment who is responsible for forestry. I would like to remind him of an
occasion when he spoke to a large major audience in the country and made the statement that he would commit the government to the national forestry policy which was laid out by his predecessor, which had as its goal the rejuvenation of the Canadian Forestry Service and, by the year 2000, an increase of 50 per cent in forest production throughout the country. The minister received cautions applause and cautions enthusiasm toward this statement.
What has the minister to report today with regard to these initiatives of his predecessor and agreed to by him? In particular, has he received a report from the multidepartmental committee which was to report in October and, if so, what is he doing to implement its recommendations?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the objectives to which the hon. member has alluded were worked out not simply by my predecessor-and I would give him full credit-but in conjunction with the provincial ministers under the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers of which, as the hon. member knows, I am now the chairman. We have been working actively with the provinces to reach those objectives. Some of the steps which we forecasted would take place have already taken place. For instance there has been, as the hon. gentleman knows, the appointment of an assistant deputy minister in charge of the forestry section of the Department of the Environment.
A whole series of studies has been undertaken by a variety of federal departments. Some of those studies have now been returned to the co-ordinating group in the Department of the Environment and others are still on their way. I could give an indication, if the hon. member wishes, of the status of each of the six studies which have now taken place, but perhaps he would prefer that I send him a letter outlining those studies.

Madam Speaker, there was no real requirement for further studies. We all know that there is a serious situation with respect to a declining forest inventory and the dire need for forest renewal throughout the country. This multidepartmental committee which was to report in October was to give the minister advice as to what initiatives could be taken by the federal government to assist the provinces and the industry to replenish and renew our forests. The report is now four months overdue. Has the minister received the report of the multidepartmental committee and, if so, is he prepared to table it? If the minister has not received the report, does he know when the report will be available for study by those who will make the decisions?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure whether or not there is a misunderstanding between the hon. gentleman and myself. The departmental committee chaired within my department has had a series of meetings. That committee has assigned a variety of subjects to a variety of departments and asked them to report to the co-ordinating committee so that it can inform me. Some of those reports from other departments have come in on schedule but one or two have been delayed
January 20, 1981

and we expect to receive them within the next couple of months.
The short answer to the hon. member's question is not as simple as he would like, but a variety of the studies that we expected to come forward have indeed come forward and we are waiting for a couple more. I am not sure if that satisfies the hon. gentleman but it is as accurate a description as I can give him of the process that has taken place.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for the interest he has shown in that answer. Madam Speaker, the question asked by the hon. member has already been discussed at some length. Privilege-Mr. Ogle

Madam Speaker, my question is addressed through you to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). As a member of the House of Commons of Canada I believe that my privilege, as well as that of other members of the House, has been infringed upon by not having received an accurate explanation or information from the Prime Minister about his recent trip to South America, Africa and Europe. I believe it is very important that this House know what went on at those meetings that the Prime Minister had with other leaders of states, because it is extremely important that this

January 20, 1981
Petition
House have accurate information on the question of North-South.
I have been a member of this House for two years and during that time we have never had a single opportunity to have a debate on external affairs, on policy, or anything like that. The 1975-80 policy of the government came to an end at the end of 1980, so we have no policy whatsoever now.
I believe it is necessary that I and other members of this House, particularly those working on North-South relations, have some kind of report from the Prime Minister so that we can at least respond to it and have an open debate in order that the country may know where we are going on this extremely important question that relates to the poor of the world. It is a situation that is becoming more and more complicated and worse for the poor. The rich are still standing back and not entering into the North-South debate with the kind of information, knowledge, and support that the poor are seeking. That is my point, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
1.	How many persons have been refused or cut off from unemployment insurance compensation because they speak only one of the official languages?
2.	Is a unilingual French-speaking claimant who moves from Quebec to a small rural town in British Columbia where the only job opportunities were for English-speaking or bilingual workers considered as not available for work?
3.	What assistance is offered to such a person who is willing to broaden his or her job search but wishes to continue to live with his wife or her husband?
4.	How many persons refused or cut off from unemployment insurance benefits for reasons of language, have had their benefits reinstated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: PERSONS REFUSED UIC BENEFITS ON BASIS OF LANGUAGE
speechtext:
1. Persons are never "refused or cut off from Unemployment Insurance" benefit on the basis of language capability.
2.	Availability for work is always a question of fact to be determined by reference to the particular circumstances of each case. The circumstances may be ones beyond the control of the claimant or ones deliberately created by the claimant. A unilingual French-speaking claimant could be disentitled because of self-imposed restrictions limiting his or her availability to an area in which the only job opportunities in the requested type of employment were for English-speaking or bilingual workers. In such a case, disentitlement would be due to the self-imposed restrictions on availability for work and not to the inability of the individual to speak English. A unilingual English-speaking claimant would, of course, be treated the same in a French-speaking area.
3.	If a Canadian migrates to parts of Canada where a different official language of work is used and cannot be placed in employment due to his or her inability to communicate in the other official language, he or she may be referred for language training under the Canada Manpower Training Program. The aim of such training is to enable the individual to obtain work in the occupation of his or her choice or in other suitable employment.
4.	Not applicable.

The House resumed, from Monday, January 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-54, to amend the statute law relating to income tax be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday when I spoke in this debate I outlined some problems which had been expressed to me by a number of people not
only in my own constituency but in a number of other constituencies across the country during the course of my travels last year. It is fair to say these concerns about income tax were expressed to me even prior to the last election. People in Canada are vitally concerned about the way in which the government redistributes the income tax it levies. Many people are asking pointed and carefully considered questions about the priorities of the government. They have asked about what role the government will play in the future in the distribution of income tax, other tax, and the management of the economy in order that we can achieve a higher level of productivity, a better distribution of wealth, and a degree of economic stability.
I was asked why it was that in 1950 personal income tax accounted for only 20 per cent of the total revenue of the country but in 1980 that figure had risen to 37 per cent. And why at the same time corporate income tax in 1950 accounted for 22.5 per cent of the total revenue of the country while now it accounted for only 10.3 per cent. I was asked why it was that people were required not only to carry the burden of inadequate management by government, but now they are being asked to carry the burden of inadequate management by the corporate sector. As I said last evening, the largest of the large in the corporate sector have now found a new way of raising money to offset the bad management decisions which they have made over a number of years. It seems as though the corporate sector has found its way into the public trough during this time. It has found a door to the treasury and it is now imposing upon the taxpayers not only the normal burden but also the cost of wrong decisions made by the boards of directors and managers of large and, in many instances, multinational corporations.
There is no doubt in my mind that there is a role for government in setting the direction the economy should take, and in co-ordinating the efforts of both private and public enterprise-I use the word "co-ordinating" advisedly-in order that we can achieve the kinds of goals which Canadians have every right to expect we should be aiming for and some day should reach.
The most often asked question is: how can it be, when a multinational company runs into difficulty, that it is able to come to the government and achieve a key to the treasury, allowing that company to obtain funds raised through personal income tax, without that company making any major commitment to an over-all economic policy and strategy, or a major commitment toward expansion and growth or toward employing Canadians now and in the future? That kind of question is very difficult to answer because the decisions are being made and, in my view, being made wrongly.
If we are going to be asked, as undoubtedly we will be in the next few years, to play a larger role in the risk areas of the funding of major corporations, and if we are going to respond positively to those requests-and I am not suggesting that in all instances we should do that-then hand in hand with those responses must go a concurrent commitment from the compa-
January 20, 1981

nies involved that they will undertake to do everything they can to secure the investment of the public of Canada.
I have always held the view that if we spend taxpayers' dollars then we should be looking at investing them, as other people do, and expecting a return on that investment. Since in many instances the investment is a significant one, we should be considering where we fit in the decision-making process on how the development is to take place and the return we expect to see not only in tax dollars but in community involvement. We cannot continue to burden the taxpayers with ever-increasing income taxes. The low and middle-income earners and workers of this country are already paying as much or more than they can afford. In some instances these people are paying far more than they can afford. Therefore they should not be asked to give the labour they are asked to give in return for the income they get and, in addition to that, to pay tax which ultimately will be channelled through the government to the very corporations which are mismanaged in the first place.
We can see today a number of sectors where we are going to be placed under severe pressure by corporate decision-makers as to whether the government will give further tax concessions, allow a more rapid depletion or depreciation, or change the rules of the game to accommodate the desires if not the needs of these corporations. I am sure that it would not surprise you, Mr. Speaker, to know that one area which concerns me greatly is that of the auto industry and what is going on within the auto industry today.
Although the auto industry representatives will not be appearing before a Senate subcommittee today because it is inauguration day, they will be appearing before that subcommittee tomorrow to place before the United States government proposals for assistance which will, hopefully, in some way rejuvenate an industry in great difficulty. At the same time as that request is being placed before the United States government, the industry will be asked to make firm commitments. These will be commitments from which no deviation can be made without permission.
It concerns me that the same industry representatives will be appearing here some day, but not before a committee of Parliament. They will be appearing in private with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). They will have one of those little fireside chats about how the government can channel further the tax moneys of the public toward assisting those corporations. But in my view when they appear, they should appear first before a committee of this House. I think they should be asked to answer some fundamental questions about the nature of the industry in order that when we are asked to take more from the people of this country by way of income tax, a larger share of their income in order to subsidize this industry, we should have before us the answers to such question as: why is it that there is such a difference between the price of an automobile in Canada and the price of the same automobile in the United States?
Income Tax Act
Why is it that instead of maximizing volume and reducing unit price they have maximized the unit price and they are, in essence, attempting to recover for themselves far more than is expected to be recovered per unit from the American consumer? This action would put people to work and give the consumers of Canada a break. I think it is vital that those questions be answered before we get around to making concessions, grants, loans, and helping to restructure the economy.
I do not know whether or not you are aware of this, Mr. Speaker, but I thought it would be of interest to you, knowing the interest you have in this matter. The average price in Canada last year of the average automobile purchased by the average Canadian rose dramatically. The average price increase this year in Canada is 36 per cent over last year. That hardly reflects an industry which is doing all it can to try to maximize sales, to encourage consumer demand to go into the marketplace and buy those products, thereby increasing the productivity and the percentage of our manufacturing capacity which is used, and thereby leading to more employment throughout this province. That would result in an increase of consumer purchasing in general.
The increase level is felt by every single major North American consumer. The average car price for American Motors this year over last year is up 34 per cent. The price for Chrysler products this year over last year is up 28 per cent. The price of Ford products this year over last year is up 40 per cent. The price for General Motors products, excluding Cadillac, is up 35 per cent. And those are the prices in Canada.
The difference between the prices of automobiles in Canada and the prices of automobiles in the United States is quite startling. The difference generally accepted by the industry as being necessary-and I am not too sure how they ever came about it-is considerable. The average price in Canada for a North American automobile is $7,061 while the same car sold in the United States goes for $6,187. That is a difference of 14.2 per cent. Those figures are with respect to the sale of the same car. In some cases the prices are considerably higher.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that the reason why people are vitally concerned about the government's expenditure program and the weight of taxation which they must carry, is because concurrent with this information goes the information that taxes continue to rise and handouts continue to be made from the government of these selfsame companies in one form or another. We must take a look at why that is. We must know for sure why there is such a differential between two automobiles manufactured by substantially the same work force with the same productivity levels and the same basic capacity to manufacture almost identical vehicles. Why is there such an outrageous difference between the sale price of a vehicle here and the sale price of a vehicle in the U.S.?
I think that is part of the management which people have a right to expect of government. I think it is part of the responsibility of members of this House to be aware of the answers to these questions. Therefore, it is part of the responsibility of government to make available to the members of the

January 20, 1981
Income Tax Act
House the opportunity to be aware of the reasons for these and other disparities which exist, before the government makes its decisions with regard to handing out taxpayers' dollars for whatever it is that management determines it needs them.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that I despair when 1 look at the programs brought in by the government. 1 fail to understand the rationale. Yesterday I attended the press conference held by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). At that press conference they, too, decided it would be appropriate to spend more tax dollars. They decided the income tax level would have to remain at least as high as it is today in order that they would have available to them some $350 million over the next three years to spend on a number of different programs.
I will not quarrel with all of those programs; it would be foolish to do so. Some of the programs are necessary and I understand that. However, I must say that I am not at all sure how they will be made equally accessible across the country. I fail to understand how the decisions with regard to which municipalities are to receive the benefits over and above those which are not, will be made.
It is obvious to me, and I think to anyone who understands economic conditions in this country, that there are more than six municipalities which are detrimentally affected at the moment as a result of recent high unemployment. Yet we are talking about providing assistance to five or six municipalities a year, for three years. One must ask which ones will be cut out? For example, is Brantford to be included? Is Sept-Iles or Sydney? Which communities will receive it? Will the decision be based on a geographic basis? Will it be required that you be a Liberal member to gain access? I would not think so, and I certainly hope not. But one asks those questions since there are no clear criteria from which to make judgments.
When I look at the program I see it is designed in exactly the same way as government programs have been designed for at least as long as I have been following government. With respect to special industry and labour adjustment programs, which are entitled New Industrial Assistance Measures, the first focus will be on firms in the designated community encountering difficulties as a result of a product or market decline or as the result of inefficient or uncompetitive production methods. As I said last night, it seems as if we are rewarding bad management. If someone comes in and says, "I was inefficient, can I get some money?" that is the person who receives it. That hardly seems the way to go about it. But that is the first focus.
The second focus refers to firms in the community which wish to expand existing operations and take advantage of new and expanding market opportunities. That makes some sense except there is one fundamental problem which confronts all of us in Canada at the moment, that is to say, we are only operating at 75, 76 or 77 per cent of our production capacity, depending on which month you talk about. We have a 22 per cent to 25 per cent unused capacity. Surely common sense tells
us that we should be striving to find markets for the unused capacity which exists. The primary focus should be to make it more attractive in the domestic market for people to purchase, and assistance should be provided in finding new markets outside Canada. In this way we can properly utilize our productive capacity which sits unused.
The program talks about firms from outside the designated community which wish to enter the community through the acquisition of, or merger with, the firm in the community. That may or may not make sense. The process one would have to go through in order to make that determination would surely be based on profit and loss, and the firm that is interested in merger or acquisition will certainly do that, with or without government assistance. In fact if there is any opportunity to make money in that field they will take it.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I know you will be interested to hear what the minister said yesterday. He was asked whether these were grants or loans, and he said they were not grants and not really loans. In fact what the program says is "negotiated repayment provisions would apply to contributions." What it means is that if you succeed it is a loan; if you fail it is a grant. That is really very silly because we have no input as to whether there will be a success or failure, no say in how it will be done, and no part in decision-making other than the granting of the money in the first place.
I want to suggest there has to be much stronger provision for reporting when we are using taxpayers' dollars. That reporting must be done to a board which has an opportunity to review, wherever it appears necessary, the structure, both financial and economic, of the company involved. There has to be an ongoing test of whether the company is living up to its commitments, whether it is in fact employing people as it said it would, and there has to be a way of recovery in the case of default.
I do not want to belabour the point other than to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the concern which is being expressed by people in the country about the level of income tax they pay, about the fact that the government is not managing the tax well, and about the fact that the private sector has now been able to gain access to the taxes paid by individual citizens in a way that heretofore it has never been able to gain access, requires careful consideration by this House. I suggest to you, sir, that the Minister of Finance would do well to spend some time talking about the criteria for expenditure as well as about the criteria for the levying of taxes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the previous member who raised a number of questions of importance under the general rubric of this bill. I cannot say I agree with all his diagnoses, but he certainly attempted to address some of the questions which are indeed right and proper to be discussed within the broad context of taxation legislation. I wish that I could say the same for a member the other evening who somehow found in the amend-
January 20, 1981

ments to the tax act that, and I quote him: "The bill will destroy our common languages, destroy our respect for democratic institutions and destroy the underpinnings of democracy itself." That apocalyptic vision of what is intended by a tax amendment bill I certainly do not share. By contrast, I would again simply note the contribution made by the previous member and recognize the serious intent of his remarks.
In any event, my purpose this afternoon is to address those parts of the bill which specifically relate to the petroleum industries. I propose to do so in the order in which those measures are presented in Votes and Proceedings for January 12.
The first three clauses of Bill C-54 which relate to the petroleum industry, 26, 27, and 28, are simply carried over from the budget presented by the previous government last December. Those three clauses were not implemented when that budget and the government itself were defeated. They do, however, reappear in Bill C-54 to give substance to the commitment of the government to alter the deduction on costs incurred in acquiring oil and gas properties from a maximum of 30 per cent to 10 per cent annually, on a declining basis. We hope that the effect of this measure, a goal which we share with the official opposition, will be to slow the bidding up of resource land values and thereby to permit the petroleum industry to put proportionally more of its revenues into the further exploration and development of our resources. I cannot, of course, promise that this desirable result will flow from this present portion of Bill C-54, but this is a goal which we share with the previous government. I trust that it continues to meet with its members' support.
With regard to other clauses of the bill that pertain to energy, I would note 44, 81 and 83 which I shall simply characterize as measures that attempt to close possible tax avoidance opportunities. All of us are, of course, aware of the remarkable imagination of some taxpayers in finding upon occasion loopholes to avoid the payment of taxes. Those three provisions are intended to prevent certain abuses, at least theoretical abuses.
Five other clauses of the bill, 90, 92, 93, 94 and 95, also relate to the petroleum industry in Canada. They are of greater significance than the three 1 have just mentioned. It is for that reason I want to take a moment to discuss them in some detail. They reflect the commitment on the part of the government to conservation and to substitution, two aspects of the National Energy Program which have not received the attention they so much deserve. Indeed, the success of the program in achieving the goal of self-sufficiency in oil for Canadians by the end of this decade will depend in significant measure on the success of the conservation and substitution commitments which are reflected in these clauses to amend the Income Tax Act.
Hon. members will recall that two important objectives of our total program, in addition to the supply side of the equation, are to ensure that we do conserve oil and that we do substitute more plentiful forms of energy for our oil resources. In this regard, members may recall that our goal is to reduce
Income Tax Act
oil consumption to 10 per cent of total energy use in the domestic, commercial and industrial sectors by 1990. Two major programs are in place to help give the private sector the opportunity to join in achieving those goals. Those two programs are the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program which is, of course, more commonly known as CHIP.
The first of those two programs, the Canadian Oil Substitution Program, will provide home owners with up to $800 to cover one half the cost of converting from oil to other energy sources, principally natural gas, but also in many areas of Canada electricity, propane, wood, and, perhaps a little later on, solar and other more unconventional forms of energy.
CHIP, on the other hand, is the principal means of providing federal funds to improve the energy efficiency of our homes. Currently households account for 15 per cent of Canada's total energy consumption. The National Energy Program provides for an increase in the total CHIP budget from about $195 million in the past fiscal year to $265 million for the fiscal year 1981-82.
I want to note for the benefit of the House the rapid growth of CHIP. It has not been without its growth problems, but the total success of that program is now evident. Certainly the increase in the number of those applying for the assistance available is reflected in the fact that in the fiscal year 1977-78 only 15,000 grants were made, whereas in the fiscal year 1981-82 there are some 500,000 grants projected at an estimated cost of some $265 million. This is a major increase in the extent and, indeed, the success of CHIP, which is given further substance in the bill before us today.
Hon. members will be aware that the goals of CHIP, that 'essential conservation program, are to reinsulate at least 70 per cent of the houses in Canada built before September 1, 1977, and, second, to achieve a one third reduction in energy used for space heating in reinsulated residences.
In our view, and I believe in the general view of the House, this program has been a successful one. It has, however, a greater role to play in the future. Is is partly for that reason that the responsibility for the policy and the financial control of CHIP will be transferred on April 1 from the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. In our view this will allow the government to stress the energy conservation aspect of the program over what might otherwise be seen as the more restricted building codes and requirements of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, I should note that the CMHC will continue to issue payments and inspect completed insulation work.
Hon. members may be aware that currently only housing units built before 1961 are eligible for grants under CHIP. It is the intention of the government, however, that eventually all houses built before September, 1977, will be eligible. The fact is, however, that at the present time only a limited proportion of the total potential number of residences which could be

January 20, 1981
Income Tax Act
insulated have in fact been insulated. The current goal will be to bring up to the necessary standards those houses built prior to 1961.
Clause 90 of the ways and means bill now before the House amends section 12(1) of the Income Tax Act as part of the legislative approval for these two important conservation and substitution programs, CHIP and the Canadian Oil Substitution Program. Rather than make these programs available only to low-income Canadians on some sort of selective basis, the government has decided instead to make them available to all Canadians without income testing. This is the most equitable and efficient way to help implement the conservation element which is such a leading feature of the total National Energy Program. However, as the bill states, the grants under these two programs must be included and reported as income for tax purposes.
If we move on to clause 92 of the ways and means bill, we find that the intent is to encourage individuals and companies outside the petroleum industry to invest in oil and gas exploration. With that provision, such an individual or, indeed, a company, is eligible to deduct exploration expenses from tax. As some hon. members will be aware, that provision has been in place since 1976, but the effect of the amendment is to extend this benefit into the future.
With regard to clause 93, I should like to take a moment because it is of real importance to the Canadian petroleum industry. In my view it reflects the flexibility of the government in implementing its energy objectives. Here we have part of the elaboration of the National Energy Program which was tabled in the House on October 28. This amendment results from representations made by the private sector, which has such an important role to play in ensuring the achievement of our energy goals.
We have heard criticism in this House and elsewhere that the National Energy Program places undue importance on the role of government. Certainly, as the chairman of Imperial Oil noted the other day, governments have and will increasingly play a leading part in the energy economy of any country. But in Canada so too will the private sector play a major part in the future energy development of our country. In this amendment we see reflected the representations the private sector has made to the government. We have found that the interests of the private sector can be accommodated within the framework of our general national energy policy.
The National Energy Program had the unforeseen effect of unduly restricting the definition of petroleum exploration expenses. We have now moved to widen that definition- loosen the definition, if you wish-so that the private sector will be eligible to deduct these expenses. For example, any dry well will be eligible for exploration expenses. Hon. members who are interested in this point may wish to refer to pages 78 to 80 of the bill. They will see there an amendment which has been welcomed by the private sector as a means of giving it greater flexibility in joining the government in achieving our common energy goals.
I might note parenthetically that the government is also working toward integrating the 8 per cent petroleum and gas revenue tax with the incentive grants system to make the program as flexible as possible for the petroleum industry. Here again I believe that we have an example of the government's flexibility in moving to meet practical suggestions made by the petroleum industry.
Clause 94 of the ways and means bill is another measure which relates to the encouragement of the active exploration in Canada for new energy supplies. Let me just explain this provision, or note this provision with an example. Let us assume that an entrepreneur invites me to participate in his drilling fund. Let us say that in December I gave him $1,000 for exploration, but the entrepreneur does not employ my money for, let us say, five years. Would I then be eligible to deduct $1,000 as an exploration expense this year? Of course not. The expense should be deducted only in the year in which the activity actually commences. The amendment in clause 94 of the bill ensures that that is the case.
By contrast, clause 95 arises from the petroleum incentives program, which makes a variety of cash incentives or grants available to the petroleum industry for the further development of our Canadian resources and in so doing, puts emphasis, on a greater degree of Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry. Both Canadian and foreign-controlled companies on Canada lands or frontier lands are eligible to receive depletion allowances at the rate of one third of exploration expenses. The same rate also applies to all companies for non-conventional and tertiary oil projects, and to crude oil upgraders. In addition to such measures, Canadian-controlled companies with at least one half Canadian ownership will be eligible for grants covering 15 per cent of exploration costs on provincial lands and one half on Canada lands. Canadian-controlled companies with more than three quarters Canadian ownership will be eligible for grants of 35 per cent on provincial lands and 80 per cent on Canada lands. The development cost grants of 10 per cent and 20 per cent respectively will apply to Canadian companies for expenditures in the non-conventional, tertiary and upgrading products.
Now that the government is moving in a decisive fashion to make incentives available to the petroleum industry, there arises a question of duplication with provincial incentives. Again let me note the intention here by providing an example. Suppose that an oilman drills in Alberta at a cost of $1 million. The provincial government gives him $400,000 for drilling and the federal government gives him $350,000. So the oilman in question spends only $250,000. But, in addition, the oilman can deduct the $ 1 million against his taxes. Assuming, as it is probably safe to assume, that he is in the 50 per cent income tax bracket, he reduces his over-all tax by $500,000. In essence, provincial and federal governments together have given that oilman $1.25 million for $1 million drilling.
This provision of the ways and means bill now before us avoids such situations by reducing the eligible expense by the
January 20, 1981

amount of any assistance which that oilman receives from another level of government.
The amendments which I have noted today in the sections of the ways and means motion pertaining to the petroleum industry might be described as secondary aspects of our total energy policy, but they do represent a further implementation of the program. Bill C-48, which is now before the national resources committee, deals with exploration and development in Canada lands. The present amendments help to provide incentives, both on the supply side and on the restraint of demand side for all of Canada. Accordingly, these amendments form an important part of our total energy policy.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should simply like to note that the energy policy incorporates a variety of goals, goals of Canadianization, of supply and of conservation. Reflected also in that policy is the proposition that investors should receive a reasonable return on their investment but that profiteering will not be permitted. Also included in that policy, and indeed in the ways and means motion before us, is that ownership rights must be respected but royalty rates should not be excessive.
In tabling the National Energy Program, indeed in legislation which we recently debated in Bill C-48 and in the ways and means motion before us, the government is moving to balance many factors in the total energy equation in Canada. I hope that others during our discussion will wish to discuss some of these points as well. In any event, I hope that by drawing attention to those aspects of the bill which relate to the petroleum industry, the House will have further evidence of the determination of the government to provide incentives to the private sector, both to conserve oil and gas as well as to find additional petroleum for the benefit of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, several years ago when the Hon. John Turner was minister of national revenue, I recall sitting in this House in Committee of the Whole dealing with the Income Tax Act. A number of members on this side of the House made certain representations to the minister requesting certain amendments to one of the clauses, and the minister agreed that he would bring forth such an amendment the next day. It was a fairly simple amendment, and one would have thought that when it came in it would consist possibly of one paragraph. However, much to our surprise, the next day when the minister presented the amendment, we found that it was some two and one half pages long and it was couched in such language that we wondered if it covered the situation it was intended to cover.
I happened to know the draftsman who drafted that particular clause and I called him and chided him for the lengthy, convoluted, and almost incomprehensible amendment. I suggested to him that it could have been drafted much more simply. The draftsman pointed out to me that because the department made use of computers, drafting of the legislation had to be done in such a manner as to comply with some arithmetical or algebraic formula so that the computer would understand it.
Income Tax Act
The situation has not changed because today we are dealing with a bill some 200 pages long containing amendments to the Income Tax Act, many of the clauses of which only the computer can understand. Yet we, as Members of Parliament, are called upon to pass judgment on these amendments, and the taxpayers who are affected by them are called upon either to interpret them themselves or else hire lawyers or accountants at considerable expense to interpret what should be a very simple provision.
I suggest to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that possibly the time has come to draft a new Income Tax Act in language not drafted for computers but for the taxpayers of this country.
Hear, hear!

The drafting should be done in such a manner that the people of Canada can understand it, in people's language, not in computer language. Not only is the legislation complicated because of computers, but I suggest the use of computers has completely depersonalized our tax system. It is becoming more and more difficult for taxpayers to receive clarification of their assessments.
For example, at one time it was fairly simple, at least in Saskatchewan, for a person who had a problem, or a client with a problem, to pick up the telephone and call the district taxation office in Regina. He could explain the problem and, generally speaking, in a matter of minutes he would have the solution. If the problem was more complicated and could not be handled on the telephone, then he could pick up the telephone and request an appointment with one of the assessors. He could drive down to Regina and the assessors were very happy to see him. They would sit down with the person, pull out the files and go over them. Generally speaking they would arrive at a solution to the problem because the files were in Regina.
There are still offices in Regina and Saskatoon, but the fdes are in Winnipeg; they have been centralized. One cannot go into Regina and see the assessor, one cannot telephone because he does not have the files. One must write a letter to Winnipeg, and if the assessor in Regina requests it, the file might filter down from Winnipeg two, three, four, five or six weeks later.
The other day I telephoned a lawyer friend and asked him for some comments about the Income Tax Act. He told me that such a simple matter as requesting an income tax clearance certificate in an estate required weeks, and sometimes months. He said that if a letter requesting the clearance was attached to the return and sent off to Winnipeg, apparently the letter requesting the clearance certificate was pulled off the return; the return went up one stream, the letter went up the other stream, and the streams never met. He said that it was a case of sending perhaps two or three follow-up letters before the income tax clearance certificate came through for the estate.
