Income Tax Act
Has the hon. minister ever given any thought to suggesting the appointment of some senior department assessors who have experience in the field to be sent out to discuss the various problems with the lawyers and accountants who, on a daily basis, are dealing with them? It would seem to me that some senior assessors, after consultation, could make some excellent recommendations to speed up the assessment of and dealing with the returns of Canadian taxpayers.
It is not my intention to go into a detailed commentary on this bill, but there are one or two points I should like to discuss. I am pleased to see that the government is repealing sections 74(3), 74(4) and 74(5). In particular section 74(3) was the one which prohibited a taxpayer from paying his or her spouse a wage or salary and deducting same as an expense for income tax purposes, unless, of course, the taxpayer was incorporated, and then it was perfectly legal. Lawyers, accountants and taxpayers could never understand the magic of incorporation-why, because of simple incorporation, one could pay his wife a wage and deduct it as an expense for income tax purposes, whereas, if one did not incorporate, one could not do the same thing. For many years the government and the tax authorities have resisted that change. It was only after pressure from members of the official opposition that such a change came about. I would say it is a change that will be welcomed in all areas of the country, whether it is in the small business field or in the farming community.
However, I was disappointed in noting that the bill gave no relief with respect to capital gains. In the Progressive Conservative government's budget of December, 1979, there was a provision which granted relief to the farming community. It did not go as far as many of us hoped, but it was well received. Unfortunately that budget never became law, but I recall in the campaign for the 1980 election that the Liberal party, in trying to gain votes and popularity in western Canada, called a news conference in Regina, with great fanfare. Some of their big guns were there and they made pronouncements on what they would do if they formed the government. They announced the double tracking of the railway, but of course no one ever thought they were serious about it. They may have been, but the producers and people of western Canada knew it was a foolish idea.
It was a lunatic idea coming from a lunatic spokesman.

No one took it seriously, but western people took seriously the undertakings of Liberal candidates that if they formed the government they would update valuation day from December 1, 1971, to 1974. There is absolutely nothing in the budget or in this bill to implement that policy. It does not look as if these promised changes will ever be implemented.
Last year when the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) tabled his budget, he also tabled a white paper entitled "A Review of the Taxation of Capital Gains in Canada". It is an interesting document, but after reading it one has the distinct impression that the authors would like to see taxation of 100 per cent of capital gains
instead of the present 50 per cent, and possibly a return to estate tax or succession duty tax, both of which were withdrawn when capital gains tax was introduced in 1972. What does the white paper indicate? I should like to look at the conclusions on page 54, and read a few excerpts. Under conclusions, the review starts off by saying:
Taxation of capital gains is an important element of the income tax system. Capital gains add to a taxpayer's ability to pay.
It goes on to say:
From various perspectives, the current tax treatment of capital gains is imperfect. Taxation of only half of capital gains, and other tax preferences that lower their effective rate of tax, are counter to the principle of tax equity-
And the review says further on in the conclusions:
Taxation of gains when realized, rather than when accrued, induces taxpayers to continue holding a particular asset longer than may be economically desirable.
Further along is says:
A number of imperfections would be removed if Canada taxed all capital gains in full as accrued.
It seems to me in reading that document that it is a move toward 100 per cent taxation of capital gains. Let us examine what has happened since the capital gains tax was imposed in 1972. There has been a rapid increase in government spending. Our budget increased from some $16 billion to over $50 billion. There has been a rapid increase in inflation of anywhere from 8 per cent to 10 per cent per year.
If we set aside gains which are made on the stock market we can see that the value of property generally has increased in step with inflation. Real property, and particularly farm land, has increased by some 300 per cent, 400 per cent, or 500 per cent. But this is an inflationary increase, not an increase in true value. As a result we end up with a tax on inflation rather than a capital gains tax.
I am concerned about the effect of capital gains tax on farm lands and small business. The capital gains tax has a drastic effect on inflating land values far beyond reason, simply because every time a farmer tries to sell a piece of land, the first thing he determines is what his capital gains tax will be, which he then adds to the asking price for the land. If the farmer gets that price for his land, then that price becomes the guiding price for all farm land in the area. When another farmer in the area sells, he asks himself the same question and determines his capital gains based on the sale price of the neighbouring farmland and, in turn, adds that to his asking price. And on it goes as land prices spiral ever upwards.
Of course tax officials and some members of the government will argue that there are roll-over provisions of which the farmer may take advantage. For example, if a farmer sells his holdings to his son or his daughter at the valuation day price, or leaves his holdings by will upon his death, then there is no capital gain. But if the farmer sells his holdings to his son or his daughter at more than the valuation day price, then there is no roll over and he must pay the capital gains tax. The situation works only if the farmer has one son or one daughter.

But if the farmer has more than one child to whom he would like to leave equal shares of his holdings, then there are problems. In most cases he ends up paying the capital gains tax, and in many cases the land is sold outside the family. As a result there are fewer and fewer family farms because of the effect of capital gains tax on farm land. Prior to the capital gains tax family farms were becoming fewer and fewer because of the effect of estate taxes or inheritance taxes or succession duties, or whatever one would like to call it.
I listened with interest on Friday to the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) when he spoke in this debate. It seems to me that the hon. member supports the taxation of wealth through capital gain and estate tax. I suggest that he and his socialist friends are rather naive. They do not seem to understand that our country was built on hard work and individual initiative, that Canadians are prepared to take risks to develop business whether it be large or small, a farm, a grocery store, a garage, a mine, or in the manufacturing industry. People took these risks to build a future for themselves and for their families. If hon. members will read page 6295 of Hansard they will find, part way down the page, the condemnation by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood of the government of 1972 for having abandoned the field of taxation of wealth by inheritance tax and estate tax. He then went on to say:
The point is that we cannot continue with a series of minor income tax proposals which fiddle here and fiddle there without recognizing that we face a major crisis, what I call a "crisis of fairness", in our tax system. I think of the people in my riding who receive their pay packet every two weeks and know exactly from where the taxes come. They see it every two weeks. They do not receive any fancy deductions, because they are employees and receive wages. They have none of the whole range of deductions which are open to those people who are self-employed, those who are able to turn themselves, as if by magic, into a personal corporation or those who are able to use a marvellous invention called the inter-vivos trust in order to split family income.
It seems to me that the hon. member does not realize that it is the self-employed, the small businessman and the large business concerns, which create jobs for his constituents through their sacrifice and initiative. In many cases the proprietors or owners of small businesses, whether they be individually-owned or incorporated, take home less pay than their employees. The employtr risks putting more money, tax paid dollars, into his business to enlarge it, to create more jobs, and to build up assets for his family and for his old age. Capital gains tax, estate and inheritance taxes, destroy and stifle the initiative that is necessary in order to expand or enlarge business and to create jobs for many constituents.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) last night and today. He condemned Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson for applying to the government for assistance. I did not hear him or members of his party say, "Let Massey-Ferguson or Chrysler go down the drain. They are the large corporations which we, as socialists, dislike and which we use as whipping boys." It seems to me that his party has been encouraging the government to grant assistance to these corporations in order to protect the jobs of
Income Tax Act
their employees. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker; they are either for the corporations or against them. They cannot blow hot and cold at the same time.
Or suck and blow.

I think it is time for members of the New Democratic Party and members of the government side of the House to examine the direction they have taken this country in the last 13 years. In those 13 years we have moved down the road toward socialism. Our productivity is down and we are rapidly losing the incentives necessary to expand our economy and to create the jobs required for our young people. The government has operated on political expediency rather than on a policy of what is good for the country.
The many give-away programs brought in by the government with taxpayers' money, higher and higher taxes and deficits that are bringing our country to the verge of bankruptcy, have taken away individual and community incentives. If the trend continues, I am afraid that instead of being one of the leading countries in the world as we were at the end of the last world war, we will become a Third World country, like those in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is taking such an interest.
I believe that these remarks should give all Canadians some food for thought, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

I would like to say "thank you" to my colleagues in caucus, Mr. Speaker. They are very understanding and perspicacious colleagues.
I am delighted to have the opportunity to follow the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). He made a point about the Income Tax Act with which I have to agree. The wording of the act is pretty difficult.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It is terrible, not difficult.

I am not sure that I would go as far as the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), Mr. Speaker. Just the other day I saw the hon. member for Portage-Mar-quette (Mr. Mayer) and the hon. member for Kamloops-Shus-wap (Mr. Riis) sitting in the hall with a copy of the Income Tax Act which they were reading through. They were chuckling and seemed to be enjoying themselves, reading it like a novel. For most of us it is a very complicated document, one which was drafted in 1972 mainly by accountants for accountants.
This brings a story to mind, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members are probably aware of the provision in the Income Tax Act application rules to the effect that when establishing a capital cost allowance base, the cost, for income tax purposes, will be neither the greater nor the lesser of A, B, or C. It is very difficult to try to figure that out as the wording is so complicated. A friend of mine went to the restaurant one morning just before he was scheduled to make a speech on the bill. When the waitress asked him how many eggs he wanted, he

January 20, 1981
Income Tax Act
replied that it would be neither the greater nor the lesser of one and three. He certainly made the point about the wording in the Income Tax Act.
She gave him an omelette.
I suggest that perhaps, as someone said about Mozart's music, the Income Tax Act is not really as bad as it sounds!
Oh, oh!

We have to consider the intent.
One of the major problems brought up by the hon. member for Moose Jaw is capital gains. He referred to the study that was made of the Income Tax Act and spoke of the needs of small business and of farmers. I should like to add some concerns that I have such as the problem of the entrepreneur, where we are going to get the tremendous amounts of money that we will require in the future to meet Canada's investment needs, and what would happen if we were to change the income tax system and increase the rate of capital gains tax.
I think one thing that we should look at very seriously is the method of raising the funds necessary to meet our investment requirements for the future. That means that if Canadians who have built up their investment in Canada are prepared to reinvest in Canada, to re-deploy their funds in this country, they should be considered in the roll-over category. In the future, we will have to reconsider how those roll overs for Canadian entrepreneurs can assist Canadians to build the type of infrastructure, the type of economy and the type of country that we will need. That is why I think it is important that the study was published. It is not government policy but it was published in order to evoke thought, to provoke ideas. This is an exercise in which we should all be involved on all sides of the House. No firm position has been taken, and the provisions have not been implemented.
There is a great disparity at the present time between the position of the New Democratic Party and the Tories on what the role of capital gains taxation should be.
I should hope so.

Perhaps that difference will have to be ironed out, but above all else the major consideration must be to meet our investment and reinvestment needs in Canada in the years ahead.
I should like to say a few words about the budget, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it is a very responsible budget in the approach adopted toward fiscal policy which involves a gradual reduction in the deficit. No one likes to see the deficit so high, but in this time of recession to have undertaken more dramatic cuts would have served to stimulate inflation further. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) so eloquently and forcefully put it, inflation is Canada's most gnawing and pressing problem.
In addition, in its approach to monetary policy the Bank of Canada, since 1975, has adopted what I believe to be a very responsible position.
Tell that to Herb Gray.
I have heard members on the other side of the House suggest that we should get away from this approach. Perhaps the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) has some different ideas.
I do.
If he thinks we should expand the money supply at a rate faster than the growth in the economy, I am ashamed of him. I do not think he would have the courage to tell that to his constituents.
Tell it to Herb Gray.
Herb Gray has never advocated that our monetary policy should be other than it has been since 1975.
That is absolute nonsense. You should have been here a year ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. It is the practice to refer to hon. members either by constituency or, in the case of a cabinet minister, by his ministry.
Absolutely. Let us have a little bit of decorum in here.

Thank you for drawing that to my attention, Mr. Speaker. I shall try to bring it to the attention of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre. I will not call him by the other names that I was thinking of.
All of which should be polite.

Very polite, but more appropriate, I think.
Based on the fiscal policy and this concept of monetary policy, this is a responsible course of action to take at a difficult time in our economic history and the economic history of all the western civilized world. If we are going to control inflation, we will do it by a gradual policy, not by any of these magical quick fixes that we have heard about. As members from the parties surrounding the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre have advocated from time to time since the budget was brought forward, it will not be by introducing a whole raft of new spending policies, even though they would like to see them.
Where we will have the most impact in helping to cure inflation is in the area of increased productivity. The budget was multifaceted. It looked at the problem of our economy from many directions. It was not just a fiscal document, it was a document which dealt with many aspects that impinge upon our economic life. I would like to cite one of them to hon. members, and then speak about it.
January 20, 1981

Since the budget was introduced, the Minister of Finance has stood up under the most scathing criticism which the opposition from both parties have been able to deliver. He still looks stronger than the day he started. His policies have stood up. They have been unable to come up with any alternatives to counter those fine policies-
He has turned grey.
He is going down the drain. He is doing just fine.
Let me quote what he said in his budget statement-
Oh, oh!
If the hon. member over there wants to discuss agriculture, I will be happy to do so afterwards.
It will be a short discussion.

These western farmers have lots of land. The eastern farmers have to farm on a much smaller acreage. Therefore we have to be more economical and more conscious of our costs, and work every inch of our soil. We do not talk in terms of sections, we talk in terms of acres. I hear the hon. member from Burlington making a comment. I invite him to help me do the chores one day. I am sure that he could show me a lot.
Another easterner putting a westerner down.

I am not putting the hon. member down. I think you are good. I am jealous that we do not have the land that you have, nor the farm income that you have. I look forward to discussing these agricultural policies when we get through with this three-hour speech I am going to deliver on the merits of our budget.
I would like to bring to the attention of hon. members the budget statement by the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen.
He is the Minister of Finance.

The Minister of Finance. I get carried away each time. The Minister of Finance said:
We intend to reduce the burden imposed on the economy by unnecessary regulation. The work of the Parliamentary Task Force on Regulatory Reform and of the Economic Council of Canada will be of great assistance in this endeavour.
That is why I am talking about the multifaceted aspects of the budget. Regulation has been defined as the means by which the government controls or determines the economic behaviour of the private sector. One of these means is through the Income Tax Act. I want to address some of my remarks to the question of federal regulations.
Our task force consisted of two members from the Tory party, one member from the NDP, and four members from the Liberal party. Incidentally, the idea of the task force was set
Income Tax Act
by the previous government, a precedent which I think was a sound one and one which I hope will be followed in the future. I give them credit for the idea.
Our task force discovered that there are 140 federal statutes and 1,608 provincial statutes which deal with government regulation of the private sector. There are over 10,000 pages of federal regulations alone. Many of them are outdated, unnecessary, and unresponsive to the needs of the private sector and the business community. Many of the regulations came into effect not through parliamentary debate, where hon. members from all sides can bring forth opinions and views of their constituents, but by order in council.
Many regulations never see debate or the light of day until they are published in The Canada Gazette. Many of these regulations come out of the multiplicity of boards and agencies which have the power to regulate and to control our lives. We have two sets of laws, those which govern and regulate us, and those which are debated here in the House. I am sure that many members opposite wish we had more laws coming through here, the way they have been filibustering some of the ones presented so far.
Our task force was faced with a number of horror stories which this multiplicity of regulations has produced respecting the impact they have had in the private sector. Let me cite one example. We found that fire marshalls' regulations said that the boiler room door of a building had to open inwards so that in the case of an explosion it would be contained. On the other hand, the fire marshall said that the door had to open outwards. With such conflicting regulations the poor contractor did not know whether to hang the door opening inwards or opening outwards. In addition, we found that 13 federal departments deal with the area of occupational health. One chemical company wanting to establish itself in Canada had to go through 43 different municipal, provincial and federal regulatory agencies before it could get a licence to operate. There were other examples of multiplicity of regulations. I can think of provincial and federal inspectors going into food processing plants, some inspecting meat and some inspecting vegetables.
In our task force report we have proposed 29 recommendations to deal with many of these problems of regulation which is, like taxation, a means of controlling our economic behaviour. We have adopted a two-phased approach. One is a consultative approach, and the other is accountability.
First, let me talk about consultation. Most of these regulations never see the light of public debate. Because Parliament is already bogged down, instead of debate we have proposed that the public servants who are consulting and regulating the private sector must enter into a consultative process before making regulations. This will involve publishing a public list of people with whom they will consult. It involves an agenda of regulatory measures which will give notice of what is coming up so the public will be informed. We hope this will involve free publication of regulations so that the private sector will have an opportunity to consult with the bureaucrats, with the public servants, and with the ministers before regulations

Income Tax Act
become law. We also hope that from the moment any public servant has an idea about a regulation, that that will go into the regulatory agenda to be published. That way regulations will not become cemented in law or the subject of partisan political advantage when it comes to trying to change them.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw entered into the debate on capital gains. This was a debate stimulated by the government publishing a study. I hope we will have more green papers and study papers and that members opposite will take them seriously and enter into debate about them.
Another aspect we feel will have an impact on slowing down the rate by which regulations are made-someone has referred to it as regulatory birth control-is the requirement of an impact assessment. Regulators will have to justify why they are regulating. The tendency whenever anyone has a problem today is to say, "Let the government fix it." We do not think this philosophy is always the best and will be applicable in every circumstance. Very often people should fix things themselves. The private sector should be concerned with fixing up a mess. This is why we want this impact assessment, to outline the problem and the possible solutions, to indicate who has been consulted, and also to show the costs and benefits to make sure that the costs of the regulations will not outweigh the benefits.
One of our approaches here is flexibility. We believe each department has different requirements. These different requirements are as a result of different constituents and the different public with which each will consult, being business, big or small, industry, labour, environmentalists, naturalists, consumers or whatever. Their requirements will be different. Therefore, within the guidelines which we have laid down, we believe each department and agency should create its own rules to meet the needs of its own particular constituents.
We are delighted with the report published by the Atomic Energy Control Board over a week ago. The AECB issued an invitation to all the people with whom it deals, to come forward and discuss with it the processes by which it will be governed. 1 would like to say that in the past this has been the practice of the Department of Finance to consult in many areas with its affected community. It has developed a good reputation, among accountants and tax lawyers, of consulting before it introduces certain measures in order to find out whether these will work or what is the best way to deal with a particular problem. I know they are doing that right now in terms of some loopholes which have been raised and discusssed in our finance committee.
The second point of this report again affects our economic performance in a fundamental way. One way I mentioned is through accountability. Our regulators, public servants and ministers who are regulating, our agencies which are regulating, should be held accountable to Parliament. This was determined unanimously by our task force. After all, we, as Members of parliament, are the ones who have to be accountable to our constituents for what goes on. We must answer to
them. This is why I think the accountability aspect will be of great interest to all members in the House.
Since Parliament is at a bottleneck under its present rules of procedure, we have made certain recommendations. For example, some people who want changes in their statutes say they have been waiting for years to get them on the Order Paper. But we have not been able to deal with them, we have not had the time. So, we will not bring every regulation before Parliament. Over the long term, what we have suggested is that the standing committees should fulfil this function. The standing committees are experienced with respect to certain subject matters. The hon. member for Portage-Marquette has been discussing this with me. He sits on the agriculture committee and he would be the one who would more appropriately be seized with the responsibility of determining what regulations are best in the area of agriculture. He should be the one to determine which areas are the most worth while and which ones should be eliminated. Over the long run the standing committee should have that responsibility.
What are the barriers to the standing committees being seized with that type of problem at this moment? In our experience the present committees are too large. They number 20 to 30 members and, as a result, a committee does not function as a cohesive whole. Discussion in a committee is often highly partisan, and this is aided by the approach that what is before it is only things that the government asks it to consider, such as bills after second reading. We do not think that even the standing committees at this stage are adequately equipped to deal with this, until serious reforms are undertaken.
Our solution is an interim committee called "A Special Committee on Regulatory Reform," which would last for only two years and would be subject to a sunset provision whereby it would disband sooner if long-term parliamentary reforms are entered into. This special committee would consist of ten members. There would be a serious limitation on substitution of members. Staff would be hired. The committee would have the power to oversee the whole process of regulatory reform and to hold public servants accountable to ensure we are cleaning up this mess of existing statutes and regulations.
We also suggest this special select committee of no more than ten members could also fulfil a second role, apart from being the force and conscience of regulatory reform. It could also serve as a model for longer-term parliamentary reform. As parliamentarians we would have a free look at how this one type of small committee with staff and dedicated members works. It might serve as a precedent for overhauling all our committees so that members could have a more effective committee system.
I think implementation of these recommendations will have a major economic impact. They would help increase the spirit of co-operation between the public and private sectors through this process of consultation. We would end up with better and more cost-effective regulations. There would be a reduced burden of regulation on the private sector. It could serve as a model of parliamentary reform.
January 20, 1981

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the experience of working together with members of the opposition on a small task force was one which was of great benefit to me personally. It was an experience I enjoyed. We had wonderful co-operation. We had very fine people working with us. I want to thank them, too, for the effort and the co-operation which they put into this report.
I think it is this type of approach, Mr. Speaker, which was embodied in the budget and is being carried through at this time by the minister and the government which will aid and assist in getting our economy moving through increased productivity, which is driven mainly by the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the very well reasoned arguments of the last speaker. I have listened as he stated with righteous indignation how he would change the whole approach to government by the party of which he is a member. He tells us how they would govern by regulation and order in council. He says there are 10,000 pages of regulations which must be changed. He says we are being strangled by regulation and that we must have changes in the rules.
The member should know that for years members on this side of the House have been making the same arguments but they have not got past first base with the government. The government has ignored them. I certainly hope that the committee, which I believe he was the chairman of, will have a greater degree of success. All of the problems he has been talking about are as a result of the Liberal approach to government, which is to keep things out of Parliament because they do not want to make Parliament too strong. They say, "Let us not change the rules because, if we change the rules, we might have to answer for some of the things we do." I suggest to the hon. member that rather than haranguing the House he should take those arguments into caucus and lay them on the table, taking the members of the government to task with those same questions. That is where we must get the action from. He will have no problems from this side of the House. We are on the record, we want to do the things he wants to do. But the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other members of the government will fight him, and fight him hard.
I am very pleased to be able to participate in the debate on Bill C-54. I will be dividing my remarks between some general comments with respect to financial matters relating to the ways and means motion and, second, commenting on some of the aspects of tax policy as they are affecting the National Energy Program, and through that program, the future outlook of supply and Canadian ownership of our oil and gas industry.
The first comment I would like to make is in relation to the direction which the government appears to be going in this budget in the area of savings and investment. There is a direction here which concerns me greatly because it appears the government is moving toward discouraging savings and the accumulation of investment capital.
Income Tax Act
I asked myself right after the budget was brought down, why it was so slim and why it was primarily energy policy. I asked why the normal budgetary elements were so very, very slim. The answer, or the conclusion, I came to was that we have only heard the first shoe; I think the other shoe is yet to fall. The initial direction which appears in this budget is that we are moving away from the directions which have been taken by the government in previous Parliaments and from the direction taken by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in his budget.
There are two things which have been removed from the December, 1979, budget, the first being the allowance to a farmer to transfer $100,000 of capital gain from the sale of a farm into a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, and the second is the provision for a Canadian common stock investment plan. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, that was to allow for contributions initially of $20,000 and subsequently $10,000, up to a maximum of $100,000 into an investment plan, and within that investment plan the income would be taxable but the capital gains tax would be deferred until the investment plan had been wound up. It allowed for the accumulation of capital and, therefore, the contribution of that capital toward the creation of jobs in this country.
The significance to me of the removal of these is that we are seeing a discouragement now of the accumulation of savings. There is no statement of intent, no statement as to why the government has chosen to exclude these from the ways and means motion. I ask myself whether this indicates a shift by the government away from encouraging savings, and I ask myself whether we have stopped there or whether we are going to carry on further into such areas as registered retirement savings plans, registered home ownership savings plans and the tax deductions of $1,000 of interest and $1,000 of dividend income.
In recent years the Canadian personal savings rate as a per cent of disposable income has been increasing, and increasing quite significantly relative to that in the United States. The figures are of the order of 5 per cent now for the United States as against about 10 per cent to 12 per cent here in Canada. In the 1960s and early 1970s it is my recollection that we were in about the same position, or possibly a little on the lower side, but because of the policies we introduced-policies which I believe encouraged saving-we improved our position. That helped in the creation of investment capital and, therefore, in the building of factories, plants and equipment. That is what creates jobs in this country and that is why it is important that we maintain these savings rates at the levels at which they have been.
If we look over the past two or three years we find that one of the primary areas of strength in our economy has been the area of private capital formation which created jobs. That was one area in which we did better than the United States. I would hope we would be able to continue to do better in the future.
The overwhelming significance of this is that in the 1980s there will be a tremendous demand for the large creation of

investment capital in the areas of energy. The figure of $200 billion is widely used as the amount of investment capital needed for this country to achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990. The next point I should like to consider is the matter of the Small Business Development Bond. This was first introduced, again by my colleague, in the December, 1979, budget. particularly of the manufacturing community in Canada. It is the sector of the economy where new big companies of the future will start. subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA BOUNDARY AND SUBMARINE LANDS
NOVA SCOTIA BOUNDARY AND SUBMARINE LANDS
speechtext:
that Bill C-226, respecting minerals and hydrocarbons in submarine lands adjoining the province of Nova Scotia, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege to present for second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works Bill C-226, which would enact the Nova Scotia Boundary and Submarine Lands Act which I had the honour to introduce in this House.
First let me say very quickly that the basic purpose of this bill is to resolve the dispute between the province of Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada concerning ownership of offshore resources like oil, gas and coal. These would also include all hydrocarbons and minerals which fall within the normal description.
How would the bill resolve this dispute? It would do so by extending the boundaries of Nova Scotia seaward from the existing coastal land mass. In the result the submarine area of the Atlantic Ocean encompassing the continental shelf, or 200 nautical miles seaward, would become part of the province of Nova Scotia.
Let me review very briefly the historical facts which give rise to the federal-provincial dispute concerning offshore resources on the Atlantic coast which are pertinent to Nova Scotia's case for ownership of those resources. King James I granted a Royal Charter to Sir William Alexander in 1621. That Royal Charter included a band of sea extending seaward for 120 miles, including Sable Island. There were subsequent treaties involving England and France which confirmed the ownership of coastal territory by Nova Scotia, over the centuries. And those treaties and agreements continued up until the time of confederation in 1867. In 1867, of course, the British North America Act confirmed, in section 7, that Nova Scotia had the same limits at confederation as before. The BNA Act also gave the provinces all land, mines and minerals which belonged to them by virtue of section 109.
It also transferred Sable Island to the Government of Canada, thus confirming and indicating that Sable Island was indeed part of the province of Nova Scotia prior to 1867. The result is that Nova Scotia claims its submarine lands and resources, and it has passed legislation to enforce those rights of ownership. In particular, Nova Scotia has passed legislation respecting coal mines and, more recently, in 1958, it passed legislation respecting the harvesting of sea plants.
Submarine Minerals and Hydrocarbons
In 1980, the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia passed the Petroleum Resources Act, which defined "Nova Scotia lands" for the purposes of that legislation. Very briefly, section 7 said that the act applied to "Nova Scotia lands", and those lands included Sable Island and the seabed and subsoil off the shores of the land mass of Nova Scotia. In addition, the Petroleum Resources Act purported to apply to the seabed and subsoil of the continental shelf and slope and the seabed and subsoil seaward from the continental shelf and slope to the limit of exploitability. So Nova Scotia very clearly, by its legislation enacted in 1980, claimed the submarine lands and the minerals, including oil and gas and coal, which might be contained in those submarine lands.
At the same time we can contrast that legislative claim of Nova Scotia with the claim made by the Government of Canada in Bill C-48 which is now before the House of Commons and which is entitled the "Canada Oil and Gas Act". The Canada oil and gas act does just the opposite. It claims to apply to "Canada lands" and defines those lands in similar terms. In the result the Government of Canada, if the Canada oil and gas act is enacted, will lay claim to ownership and exercise jurisdiction over that area of the submarine lands adjoining Nova Scotia, extending seaward for 200 nautical miles and including the continental shelf. So the problem is evidenced by the passage of those two pieces of legislation: in Nova Scotia, the Petroleum Resources Act and, in the Parliament of Canada, the Canada oil and gas act.
The dispute with respect to ownership of offshore lands and resources must be resolved. Why must it be resolved? It must be resolved because we hear reports daily that it is delaying and hindering the development and exploitation of our natural resources off the coast of Nova Scotia and off the coast of Newfoundland.
Reports have indicated that executive officers of the Mobil Oil Company, which heads the syndicate exploring off the coast of Nova Scotia and off the coast of Newfoundland, have said time and time again that the continuance of this dispute and the failure to resolve the dispute concerning jurisdiction over offshore resources will delay and hinder future development and exploitation of those very resources.
How can this dispute be resolved? Of course, always by negotiation and agreement between the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces affected by this dispute. However, for years such negotiation has failed to resolve the matters in issue.
On October 28, 1980, the National Energy Program was introduced in this House. The documents comprising that National Energy Program refer to this dispute. Briefly stated, the dispute was sought to be resolved by the Government of Canada giving to the provinces which have coastal lands 75 per cent of the wealth which would result from the development of those lands and resources. That was not acceptable to the provinces involved, and similar attempts to negotiate other arrangements have failed. What can we do to resolve the dispute? There is one other method, and that is to refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada.

January 20, 1981
Submarine Minerals and Hydrocarbons
However, 1 think parliamentarians, and all Canadians, would agree that this is a very poor way to resolve an intergovernmental dispute. 1 believe the dispute is constitutional in nature because it arises from provisions in the British North America Act and from the arrangements which were made between the provinces which originally formed the confederation which became the Canada we know today. Because of that I think it should be resolved outside the courts. If it cannot be resolved by negotiation between governments, it ought to be resolved by the Parliament of Canada to the extent that the Parliament of Canada has the necessary jurisdiction and capability to resolve the dispute.
We know that all the provinces of Canada, as a result of meetings between them and at the first ministers conferences, have agreed to provincial ownership of offshore resources. With that in mind, we know that if the Parliament of Canada acts in this area, unlike the constitutional decisions that have been taken by the government, we will act with the consent and concurrence of the provinces of Canada.
Under section 3 of the British North America Act of 1871, the Parliament of Canada clearly has the authority to extend the boundary of a province. This is what Bill C-226 proposes. It will extend the boundaries of the province of Nova Scotia pursuant to the authority granted by that section. Of course, the result of extending the boundaries in this manner will be that the resources contained in those submarine lands will then vest in the province of Nova Scotia. This technique is similar to that used in relation to the extension of boundaries of other provinces, including the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. A better example, however, is the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba in 1912 by the Manitoba Boundaries Act which was enacted by the Parliament of Canada.
The bill which I am proposing in the House today for second reading follows the precedent of the Manitoba Boundaries Act. As I have said, it extends the boundaries of Nova Scotia, it defines the area involved in the extension, and it provides for the specific location of those boundaries by the executive authority. At the same time it preserves existing rights in submarine lands and, as required under the British North America Act, it provides for the consent of the province of Nova Scotia to the extension.
I have said that the dispute between the province of Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada with respect to offshore ownership must be resolved. I have said that it is slowing and hindering the pace of exploration of the resources off the coast of Nova Scotia, and certainly it is slowing the pace of the investigation and of the exploration off the coast of Newfoundland because officers of Mobil Oil have said so time and time again. But more important, the exploration of our offshore resources in Nova Scotia has a tremendous effect on the resolution of our energy problems in the province. As has been pointed out to the House time and time again, Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces are at the whim of the foreign powers which supply oil through the OPEC agreement.
In Nova Scotia we pay the world price for oil, and this has a disastrous effect on the cost of electricity generated through the use of oil-fired thermal units. So we have to move to resolve these problems. We are doing so in the province of Nova Scotia in a number of ways. First and foremost is the conversion of oil-fired thermal units to coal and the development of the coal mines and resources which accompany that change. Second, we have instituted pilot projects to develop tidal power on the Annapolis River, and we hope that some day we will be able to develop tidal power in the Bay of Fundy. In addition, we seek the extension of the natural gas pipeline from Quebec to the Atlantic coast and to Nova Scotia. The fourth possibility is the use of natural gas delivered to the province of Nova Scotia by some other method. However, our long-range plan and our hope for the future is in the exploration and development of offshore resources.
I believe that Nova Scotia's energy future is dependent on the development of offshore resources, just as much as it is dependent on the delivery of natural gas to Nova Scotia, on the development of tidal power, or indeed on coal conversion. So I think that the failure of the Government of Canada to act to resolve this dispute is having an adverse effect on Nova Scotians and on all Canadians, because under our petroleum subsidization program all Canadians are called upon to support the price of oil delivered to the east coast of Canada and utilized in the maritime provinces and in Quebec.
The extent of this subsidy at the present is $3 billion a year. As you know, the actual subsidy program involves the Government of Canada paying the difference between the world price or the OPEC price for oil and the price for Canadian oil which prevails at the time of the delivery. As I have said, this subsidy program is costing millions and millions of dollars a day and is a drain on the resources of Canada, so it is in the interests of all Canadians to resolve these problems. One way to resolve them is to settle the offshore resources dispute so that the companies and the private sector involved and interested in offshore exploration can get on with their work and produce the results we all seek.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and members of the House for their indulgence. Let me point out again that while Bill C-226, which enacts the Nova Scotia Boundary and Submarine Lands Act, appears to be a local matter, it is indeed a matter of national significance because I believe it would resolve the federal-provincial dispute with respect to offshore resource ownership which will enable the quick development of our offshore resources, thus resolving in part the energy problem in Nova Scotia.
I know that other colleagues of mine on this side of the House, particularly the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), will want to make a contribution to the debate on Bill C-226, and I will yield the floor in the hope that members will see fit to give this bill second reading.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA BOUNDARY AND SUBMARINE LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-226 is clearly to extend the boundaries of Nova Scotia to the greater distance of the continental margin. I shall want
January 20, 1981

to address that point in a moment. Before doing so, however, I want to say how many points the hon. member opposite made with which we on this side of the House agree. While I do not intend to support his bill, for reasons which I believe will become evident, I do want to say that we agree with him that the differences between the government of Nova Scotia, and indeed of Newfoundland, and the national government should be resolved by negotiation. Failing that, there is the route of reference to the Supreme Court, but it continues to be our view that, if possible, this disagreement should be resolved, as the hon. member has suggested, by negotiation.
I also agreed with the hon. member when he outlined some of the energy projects that can be taken to benefit the people of the maritime region, from where my ancestors came. I have in mind particularly his comments about the extension of the Q & M pipeline, a policy which the government fully supports and which is an important aspect of the National Energy Program.
As stated in that program, the government believes that the ownership of the territorial seas is vested with the federal government, as are the rights and responsibilities conferred under international law out to the 200-mile limit. It is the right of the national government to dispose of or exploit the natural resources situated in those submarine areas adjacent to the coast of Canada. Indeed, the Supreme Court confirmed this when it judged that beyond the lower water marks and outside the inland waters, the Government of Canada owns the area, has a right to exploit and explore it and has legislative jurisdiction over it.
However, the government, although committed to the proposition that large revenues generated from the exploitation of natural resources must benefit all Canadians, also recognizes that substantial benefits should go to the provinces. In that connection, I recall the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the last election campaign at Memorial University in Newfoundland, when he made a clear commitment on the part of the national government to ensure that the people of the coastal provinces and in the maritime region received the full benefit of the potential riches which should flow from the development of offshore resources.
The National Energy Program indicated that the government is anxious to resolve the ownership issue, if necessary, through the Supreme Court for many of the same reasons which the member opposite mentioned. It read:
-uncertainty about the legal control over such vital areas is not conducive to the rapid development of the oil and gas potential of this promising region.
It might be useful to look for a moment at the efforts made in recent years to correct this situation. As early as 1976 the government indicated its willingness to proceed with a joint reference by both the provincial government and itself to the Supreme Court to have the matter settled. The government has been awaiting the approval of Newfoundland in such a reference. In the case of Nova Scotia, its provincial government has consistently indicated that it did not wish to address
Submarine Minerals and Hydrocarbons this issue in the Supreme Court but, as the hon. member opposite indicated, would rather reach an agreement through discussion and negotiation.
Ownership is not the only issue, and in the particular case of Nova Scotia it appears not to be the key issue. The government of Nova Scotia puts more emphasis on the following issues: first, the management and administration of offshore resources; that is, the rights to issue licences, leases, permits and so forth; second, the control of the pace of development of offshore resources; third, the possibility to determine the conditions under which goods and services are supplied to the industry in order to obtain a share of these business activities; fourth, the ability to provide preference in hiring for Canadians living in Nova Scotia. I must say that this last point would give me some difficulty. Those issues have formed the heart of negotiations over the past several years. However, the government of Nova Scotia clearly indicated in the past its confidence in having the matter resolved through negotiations with the federal government.
I should like to refer to the memorandum of understanding of 1977 between the federal government and the maritime provinces in which Ottawa proposed a provincial 75 per cent and a federal 25 per cent split of offshore resources revenue. The government was prepared to bear all costs of administering these areas. The 1977 proposal was rejected only by the government of Newfoundland. However, in 1980 the government of Nova Scotia terminated its earlier agreement of 1977 and claimed offshore ownership. On that basis, it introduced the legislation which the hon. member opposite mentioned- the petroleum resources act, the pipeline act, the gas utilities act and the energy and mineral resources conservation act.
In September, 1980, the question of natural resources and offshore resources ownership was on the agenda of the first ministers' conference on the constitution. Several options were reviewed at that time. While Nova Scotia reiterated its claim, interest was expressed in examining administrative mechanisms to resolve the issue. I should like to quote from page 43 of "The National Energy Program" where it refers to the efforts in September to reach agreement. It reads as follows:
Seeking a speedy and fair resolution to this issue, the Government of Canada offered to:
Provide 100 per cent of provincial-type resource revenues to the adjacent province, subject to arrangements whereby, when the province reached an agreed level of wealth, these revenues would be shared with other Canadians. Give the provinces a substantial voice in matters of direct concern to them, including in particular the need to minimize social, environmental and economic disruption in the region.
Unfortunately, the offshore resource issue was not resolved.
Following the September discussions which I just mentioned, the Premier of Nova Scotia made a distinction between his position and that of Newfoundland. I refer hon. members interested in this subject to the October 31 edition the Chronicle-Herald of Halifax which indicated that the premier, while still wanting 100 per cent of the benefits from offshore oil and gas to go to the province, thought the ownership question "can be put aside". Given the premier's viewpoint of a few months ago that ownership can be put aside and his concurrent view

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA BOUNDARY AND SUBMARINE LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for his foresight and loyalty as a Nova Scotian in bringing forward this piece of legislation to espouse a very just cause and to establish an important principle.
I think it would be useful to remind the House, as did the editorial which appeared in the Chronicle-Herald of Halifax some months ago, of some of the historic bases for the claims of the maritime provinces for greater equity in participating in the submarine resources adjacent to these provinces. I listened to the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) who, I think, said at one point that this did not espouse a very constructive course of action and intimated that we had not made a particularly great contribution. I do not want to misquote him, but I want to emphasize that we in the Atlantic region, particularly those of us in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, have some very valid historic claims to our undersea resources.
Also the parliamentary secretary referred to the 200-mile limit. I think it is true-and my opinion is shared by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who is a most knowledgeable Member of Parliament on questions of energy and offshore resources-that the international law which is still relevant dates back to a 1958 law of the sea conference whereby Canada sponsored a resolution indicating that littoral states had sovereignty over their offshore lands on their submarine shelves, slopes, coastal flats, and so on.
As far as that goes, they had unlimited sovereignty until they were met by the claims of the other littoral states, even if they were many hundreds of miles away. I believe enough states ratified this convention so that it is still international law. Despite pressures which have not yet culminated in changing the international law, that is still the case.
With regard to our contribution to confederation, I would like to quote again from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald editorial. It might be constructive to acquaint the House with just what happened with respect to the Atlantic provinces as opposed to what was done for many other Canadian provinces. The article reads in part:
Prior to the creation of Saskatchewan and Alberta as provinces in 1905, and the enlargement of Manitoba, Quebec and Ontario a few years later, the lands that Ottawa gave those provinces were mutually owned by all Canadians,
including the three maritime partners in Canada-Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Not only were the maritimes required to relinquish rights to lands and resources in which they had previously held shared entitlement, they were not considered, consulted or compensated. Geographically disadvantaged, in that they are not butted by northern lands, they remained small in area, receiving no additional territory.
It is interesting to look at the respective geographical areas of our provinces. Prince Edward Island has only 2,000 square miles, Nova Scotia 21,000 square miles, and New Brunswick 28,000 square miles; as compared to the other provinces in Canada such as Quebec which has 595,000 square miles, Ontario 412,000 square miles, Manitoba 251,000 square miles, Saskatchewan 252,000 square miles and Alberta 255,000 square miles. The latter group of provinces was created out of lands which were the joint property of the maritime people and the maritime provinces.
As to making contributions, I am reminded of a story. A pig and a chicken, while sauntering down the street saw an advertisement in the local restaurant which said "Bacon and eggs, 69 cents!" The chicken said to the pig, "Isn't it wonderful, the economic contribution we are making?" The pig said, "To you it may be a contribution, but to us it is a total commitment." The maritime provinces have made a very great commitment, not only by coming into confederation under terms which disturbed our previous prosperous state when we were world traders and a major maritime power, but under terms which grafted us on to the then troubled colonies of Upper Canada and Lower Canada, and we have been disadvantaged ever since.
The approach espoused by the hon. member for Halifax West gives the Government of Canada an opportunity to do what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain and his government of that day attempted to do, to give every region in Canada rough equity so that they can realize and be endowed with resources which will help them to grow and strengthen the total economic face of our nation, as opposed to the approach, as the hon. member for Halifax West has pointed out, in Bill C-48. His bill C-226 provides for a positive approach to strengthen our country by making available to areas of Canada that have been disadvantaged in the past, out of resources that are available, additional territory to bring their areas into a more equitable balance with some of the other provinces which had their territories increased some years ago.
There is no difficulty for such a move in so far as the precedents are concerned. The hon. member for Halifax West cited the British North America Act. One neat and tidy technique would be to follow the precedents in our constitutional history, some of which are the Canada and Ontario Boundary Act of 1889, the Ontario Boundaries Extension Act of 1912, the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912 and the Manitoba Extension Act. There is also the Alberta Act of 1905, the Saskatchewan Act of 1905, the Alberta Natural Resources Act of 1930 and the Saskatchewan Resources Act of 1930. Surely there is no lack of constitutional historic precedent for taking that move.
January 20, 1981

It is interesting to highlight and contrast the approach as epitomized by my colleague and that of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). On the one hand the government under Bill C-48 is taking hydrocarbon resources away from not only the territories, which is bad enough, but prematurely, before court action, from some of the senior provinces in confederation. It is not merely the simple act of taking these resources away which bothers me, but the attitude which can be found in the proposed Canada lands act.
There is a tremendous amount of discretion of a totalitarian nature in this bill. I will cite only one section of the proposed Canada lands act which bothers me in this respect, and it is with regard to the assessment of royalties. Clause 43(9) reads:
Proceedings in an appeal to the Federal Court of Canada under subsection (5) shall be held in camera on request made to the court by a party to the appeal.
Subsection (5) deals with royalty disputes. As a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, I sense that this must trouble you as well. This particular piece of legislation also talks about privilege. But to come back to the attitude and posture of this government, why in the world would a party to an appeal to our Federal Court in this country be directed-and there is no choice, the court is told-to hold proceedings in camera. Is this piece of legislation equivalent to the Official Secrets Act? Are we getting back to the same kind of infamous section which we see in the Federal Court Act, section 41(2)? This is the kind of attitude which troubles me, apart from the idea of taking away from the residents of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon valuable natural resources which is bound to impede their progress toward provincial status.
It is worse for the people in my own province and the Atlantic region to see our historic grants which were given to us, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Halifax West, by James I hundreds of years ago being totally ignored, as this government is ignoring the territorial claims of Newfoundland which were laid out when that province joined confederation. Then the government draws boundaries around our offshore lands and directs, thanks to this unparalleled ministerial discretion, any oil company, great or small, multinational or Canadian, as to where they shall drill, when production shall start, where the oil shall be stored, where it will be transported, where it will be refined, when it will be sold and what they will receive for it. Is that the kind of development which will help exploration take place in our offshore areas in Atlantic Canada and our territorial lands? 1 do not think so.
I do not believe that Bill C-48 can stand as it is presently drafted. I do not believe that any self-respecting company, whether it be in the petroleum industry or any other industry, would willingly work under such strictures. I see this Bill C-48, as opposed to the kinds of approaches espoused by the hon. member for Halifax West, as wrecking the chance for this country to develop the trillions of dollars needed to get us out of the unholy financial mess in which we find ourselves. I see it wrecking our chances for energy self-sufficiency, and I see it as being directly opposed to the traditional tenets of helping
Submarine Minerals and Hydrocarbons regions, helping people develop and giving them the resources to work with themselves.
After all, what the hon. member is asking for and our province follows the same philosophical approach that was once available to individuals, and still may be available in certain parts of this country, when lands were granted to people on the understanding that they would improve them, develop them and pay taxes on them for the greater good of the country. Surely, this kind of approach is preferable to this arbitrary, totalitarian grab for resources which is implicit in Bill C-48. 1 know, as the parliamentary secretary has said, that there are many problems inherent in a statute such as Bill C-48. There are bound to be some very tough negotiations as to what would be encompassed in these increased territorial grants to the provinces and the Atlantic region, but that can be worked out. It is not a great problem.
The attitude of this government is a problem, Mr. Speaker. This has been highlighted by putting the government on the spot by means of Bill C-226, and by pointing out that there is a just and equitable way to increase the economic potential and to redress past wrongs against the Atlantic provinces.
I commend this bill to the House of Commons. I hope my colleagues will give it sympathetic consideration; not talk it out, but let it go to the committee to see if it may not be the means of developing a different approach to offshore mineral and hydrocarbon development in the Atlantic region.
You probably know, Mr. Speaker, that at this very moment coal is being mined several miles off the coast of Cape Breton Island. This is not a very large precedent, but it illustrates there is no reason why a territorial grant of a substantial amount could not be made to benefit the Atlantic region. It would not affect navigation, fisheries or the rights of other maritime nations but it would greatly strengthen Canada's position in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in the debate this afternoon and to support the substance of the bill before us. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) who proposed the motion. I believe it identifies the very real problem that affects confederation and proposes a solution which is quite commendable.
In 1867 when Canada was formed, our land area was only a fraction of what it is today. British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland were not part of the dominion. The northwest, stretching from Lake Superior to the Rockies, was owned by the Hudson's Bay Company.
Two months after the dominion was formed in the federal election of 1867, anti-confederationists captured 18 of the 19 seats in Nova Scotia. Indeed, the following year a delegation of Nova Scotian politicians travelled to London to seek the repeal of the British North America Act. Two years later, in

January 20, 1981
Submarine Minerals and Hydrocarbons
1869, the Eludson's Bay Company agreed to sell its vast territory, which included the future provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to the new Dominion of Canada for $1.5 million. Unhappy westerners who wanted no part of the new country instituted a rebellion under the leadership of Louis Riel. That is a moment in Canadian history. The creation of Manitoba followed, and Saskatchewan and Alberta were created in 1905.
Significantly, at the time of the Eludson's Bay sale of land to Canada, there were only four provinces, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec-Upper and Lower Canada. We might make a case that both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick had a one quarter interest in the newly-acquired land that was later erected into our western provinces.
It is a matter of history that in 1912 Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec were greatly expanded to include the lands to their north which were very thinly populated and essentially unsettled. The maritime provinces, on the other hand, had been land-locked and could not be similarly expanded.
I therefore suggest that New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have an historic claim to that portion of the continental shelf that is owned by Canada and which joins their respective coast lines. A similar case can be made by Newfoundland.
The additional lands given to Quebec and Ontario just about doubled their land area, while the northern expansion of Manitoba to include parts of Keewatin, and the addition of parts of Athabasca and Assiniboine to Saskatchewan, more than doubled their original land areas. The addition of part of Athabasca to Alberta in consequence of its northern expansion just about doubled its land area.
In my view, it is quite significant that the tremendous resource wealth in these provinces is to be found to a great extent in the northern territories added to the original provincial boundaries. The pre-Cambrian shield around Hudson Bay in northern Ontario, the spectacular resources in northern Quebec and the energy resources in the western provinces are cases in point.
The natural area of expansion for the maritime provinces is in the coastal areas adjacent to their boundaries. In my view, the case is well made for the maritime provinces to have their boundaries expanded to include the coastal areas under the sea.
The maritime provinces have an historic, legal and moral claim to these areas. So, too, has Newfoundland. The Atlantic provinces, together, suffer problems related to regional disparity. One half of their provincial revenues are now in the form of transfer payments from the federal government.
I suggest to the House that the wealth contained in the offshore resources would help alleviate these problems and would certainly strengthen confederation. I should therefore like to support the bill introduced by the hon. member for
Halifax West whom I hold in great esteem and I congratulate him for introducing it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this subject can be approached from a very non-partisan point of view. In 1957 I took over as minister of resources or, as it was called then, national resources and northern affairs. This was a new department of government which was created in 1953 because we had been regarding our north and other resources with a kind of absence of mind.
When checking through the records of that new department in 1957, I discovered evidence that the problem that has been raised today by the hon. member was already in the minds of the administration of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. I spoke to the then leader of the opposition about it from a legal point of view, as he was very proud of his background and experience in that field. He said that he thought the only way we could expand the territories of the Atlantic provinces was to divide up the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Being a considerable authority on constitutional matters as well as matters of law, he proposed that the boundary line of the Gulf of St. Lawrence should run from Anticosti Island in the north, down to the Gaspe.
I enlarged on that idea, Mr. Speaker. I knew that the Department of External Affairs and my own department of northern affairs, in co-operation with all the other nations of the world, were working on what was called the international geophysical year. There was a worldwide conference which lasted two or three years, although it was only supposed to last a year and one half. I knew the kind of information that was being fed into that conference. The theory of how the continents were formed had changed dramatically from previous beliefs. All the current theories were being questioned. It was realized that the eastern seaboard of North America was once part of Europe, that we had been drifting apart and that the geology of the Appalachian region which runs from Greenland, through Baffin Island, down through the Labrador trough, the Atlantic provinces and into the northeastern United States, has the same geology as that of western Europe. The coal and iron mines of Germany, Sweden, Luxembourg, France and Great Britain are of the same structure as the coal and iron mines of the Appalachian region.
It was also abundantly clear, as the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has pointed out, that this wealth does not stop at the high water mark but continues underneath the sea.
As part of the vision of the Diefenbaker period, we thought we could give the Atlantic provinces an equal chance with the prairie provinces, Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia by giving them enough territory with resource potential. We thought we could also give them an industrial strategy by combining in that area all the forms of energy we could get. For instance, coal, iron from the Labrador trough and the give-away gases from Venezuela, which we could get for long-term agreements at almost nil prices. We could build into
January 20, 1981

that whole structure an energy network which would give this part of Canada, with perfect position for trade purposes with Europe, Africa, South America and the Eastern Seaboard of the United States, with access to supply from the Arctic as well as the Labrador trough, one of the great potential mineral areas of the world, some form of hope for the future.
I visited various governments, including Quebec. 1 suggested that we consider such a scheme. I wanted to include Gaspe because geographically it is part of that whole picture. Gaspe could tie up with the Labrador trough. An energy network could be built crossing from Cape Breton to Newfoundland to Labrador, picking up the power in the Hamilton River, and bring it down to Quebec City, Montreal and New York. We could develop the Fundy tides, develop the coal and use the cheap energy from Venezuela. We could then build an energy base which would economically give that area one of the strongest that any industrial complex could have.
It is rather difficult when you first make a proposition like that to have unanimous support among administrative governments which are busy with their problems. All I could get out of that first round of discussions was what appeared on the books in this House in 1957, which was the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act.
I repeat again, that act was not called an act for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, it was called the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. I had the pledge of the Quebec government that it would co-operate to develop and participate in this industrial complex. In the actual act passed by this Parliament, as hon. members will see if they go back to read it, we were only able to arrange anything tangible with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That was the Beechwood project on the Saint John River, and the tying up of the two grids into a bi-province grid. We had long discussions with the province of Newfoundland about building that grid into Newfoundland and getting access to the power in the Hamilton River. All of this is history, but very important as a backdrop to what is in this motion today.
We missed our opportunity 20 years ago because there was a reluctance to give up that tremendously strong and historic pride which each of those island areas have. Nova Scotia is an island, connected a little bit with New Brunswick, Cape Breton is an island and so is Newfoundland.
However, I think I have said enough to point out that even though we did not succeed in achieving our full purpose in 1957-1958, we did succeed in going to the Law of the Sea Conference in Geneva and fighting hard for the fishing rights, along with all of the other causes we fought for, and we got unanimous approval that the littoral state could develop the resources at the bottom of the sea as far out until you met the other nation coming from the other side of the ocean with the technology of the time. That is the international law today, which was pointed out by the hon. member for Central Nova. We should take advantage of this opportunity even though it is 20 years later. We should push this idea forward because it is

unfair and inequitable to leave four eastern provinces which have not received the same treatment as British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec have received out of this federal system and I think this motion could advance things very rapidly.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will be brief. Bill C-226 introduced by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) interests many from Atlantic Canada but, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said, its dimension is much wider than just the geographical parameters of Atlantic Canada. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) gave a historical review of the expansion of other provinces where a lot of the natural resources are now. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) in his development of this matter shows the very real interest in it. But what has never ceased to surprise me in terms of the federal position versus the Nova Scotia and provincial position is that under our tax sharing proposals now and/or the equalization grants-let alone the cost of these imported oils-it is almost six of one and half a dozen of the other. If a province can develop that offshore mineral resource and thereby get the benefit and the money from it, then in time Nova Scotia or another province will become a have province in terms of the expected potential wealth. This will help offset what the federal government is paying now under the equalization formula. I was interested in the historical background which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain described. There is no doubt, as the hon. member for Halifax West said, the conflict has impeded development and we are losing out with this constitutional conflict on the shore.
I would just like to add that with the extension of the provincial boundaries, this will enable a province to develop its resource, in which all Canadians share. For instance, if the Nova Scotia revenue base is better, that province will then need less input and/or subsidy from many subsidized programs, let alone the basic equalization formula. Somewhere along the line I hope that the mandarins of the world will get together and say let us not impede development, let us expand it so that all Canadians can benefit. I compliment the hon. member for Halifax West for bringing to the attention of the House something which rankles eastern Canadians. We know at the moment there are more resources developed in the west. We do not begrudge them that. We obviously benefit from it in terms of sharing. We do not deplore the fact that as four of the original partners, the boundaries were extended to the western provinces and although we have a vicarious ownership in that land being part of the original entity, we are not small-minded Canadians. As the boundaries were extended for provinces in the west, and Quebec had its boundaries extended north, under the various statutes of this House, all we ask for Atlantic Canada is that we be treated the same by having the only land we have, which is under the sea, extended as proposed by the hon. member for Halifax West.
